@@138590515 <h> Key points <p> To resist authoritarianism and govern AI well , we must design systems that fit human nature , not reject it . <p> In 1924 , the psychologist John Watson made a famous offer . Give me a dozen healthy infants , he wrote , and I will train any one of them to become any specialist I choose -- doctor , lawyer , artist , even thief -- regardless of talent or ancestry ( Watson , 1924 ) . It was the boldest version of one old answer : a human being is raw material , and culture does the shaping . <p> The opposite answer is just as old . Hobbes ( 1651 ) described people in their natural state as selfish and dangerous , like wolves to one another . And the impulse survives in modern dress , in headlines that promise a " gene for " intelligence , faith , or crime . Between Watson 's blank slate and the gene-for-everything story sits a question argued about since antiquity : Is there such a thing as human nature , or are we whatever @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first answers , and each reduced us to a single layer . Aristotle called us the rational animal ; reason was our essence . The Stoics told us to live in accordance with nature . Rousseau ( 1755 ) replied to Hobbes , arguing that people are born gentle and corrupted by society . Instinct or environment , essence or construction -- every portrait picked one . And each , we now know , was too simple . <p> What Darwin Started <p> Darwin changed the terms of the argument . His point was not that humans are noble or base , but that we are one species among many , shaped by the same selection pressures as everything else alive ( Darwin , 1871 ) . That move took us off the pedestal . It also raised a harder question : If natural selection built our bodies , what did it leave in our minds ? <p> The modern answer is that we carry not one but two inheritances . Alongside our genes runs a second system -- culture : language , norms , tools , institutions , passed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1985 ) called this gene-culture coevolution , and Henrich ( 2020 ) has shown how far it reaches . Genes shape what culture can build , and culture , over time , reaches back and reshapes the genes themselves . <p> Dual inheritance <p> Source : Onurcan Yilmaz <p> Two Inheritances That Rewrite Each Other <p> It helps to separate the two kinds of adaptation because they are easy to confuse . In the first , the environment does the pushing . Take skin color . Near the equator , strong sunlight can harm the body , so darker skin , which shields against it , was favored ; farther north , where sunlight is weaker , lighter skin helps the body produce enough vitamin D ( Jablonski and Chaplin , 2000 ) . Nobody chose this . The sun was there , and bodies adjusted to it . <p> The same holds elsewhere . Tibetan highlanders carry gene variants that let them thrive in thin mountain air ( Beall , 2014 ) , and the Bajau " sea nomads " of Southeast Asia have unusually large spleens , an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2018 ) . Nature set the challenge , and biology answered . <p> The second kind of adaptation is stranger , because the pressure is something people invented . Most mammals stop digesting milk after infancy , when the body switches off the enzyme that breaks down lactose . But once some human groups began herding animals and drinking their milk , adults who kept producing that enzyme had an advantage , and over generations the trait spread ( Gerbault and colleagues , 2011 ) . What drove the change here was not a climate but a custom people had invented , and over time , that custom reshaped the genome itself . <p> Diet keeps leaving such marks . Among the Inuit , generations of eating fish and sea-mammal fat selected for gene variants that change how the body handles fat , down to the omega-3s people now buy in capsules ( Fumagalli and colleagues , 2015 ) . And as farming spread and starch filled the plate , the number of copies of the salivary amylase gene increased in parallel ( Perry and colleagues , 2007 ) . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ eat with . <p> Culture can even reach into the brain . Learning to read , invented only a few thousand years ago , reorganizes part of the visual cortex ( Dehaene , 2009 ) . Sometimes the force is an institution : when the medieval Catholic Church banned marriage between cousins , it dissolved Europe 's dense kin networks and , over centuries , nudged whole populations toward individualism and trust in strangers ( Schulz and colleagues , 2019 ) . Each of these is culture rewriting biology , not taking turns with it . <p> Neither Essence nor Blank Slate <p> Neither extreme holds . Human nature is not a fixed essence but an evolving design space : a set of biological capacities continually structured , extended , and redirected by cultural institutions . Our genes set the boundaries , the range of what is possible ; culture decides which possibilities actually open . A child learns to speak with almost no instruction because language sits near the center of that space . Calculus has to be taught because it sits at the edge . Flapping our arms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this is only a question for biologists . Get the diagnosis of human nature wrong , and you design the wrong society . Treating the mind as a blank slate , ignoring biology in medicine , and ignoring culture in politics -- these are the same mistakes in different clothes . <p> Today 's hardest problems make the stakes concrete . Authoritarian movements do not invent new drives ; they take old ones -- our quick , evolved alarm at threat and uncertainty -- and channel them , and whether they win depends on the institutions around them ( Acemoglu and Robinson , 2012 ) . Artificial intelligence is becoming what writing and the printing press once were : a new force in cultural evolution , except that it now produces and selects information , not just carries it . <p> The climate crisis runs straight into a mismatch . Minds built to react to immediate , concrete dangers struggle with a slow , abstract one . Markowitz and Shariff ( 2012 ) found that framing climate change as a moral responsibility , rather than a technical chart , moves @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fairness and the claims of future generations , not by data alone . Human nature is not a cage . New norms and institutions are how our species has always handled problems its biology never prepared it for . But those fixes work only when they are built on an honest picture of the people they are meant to serve . <p> One of my supervisors , Hasan G. Bah ? ekapili , used to tell me that you can not change human nature ; only nature can do that . He was right , and I would only add what follows from his point : what we learn about human nature can still change what we build with it . The room to choose our direction is real . It simply runs through our nature , not around it .

@@138621130 <h> An AI that Predicts but has no Hidden Agenda : LawZero Lays out a Formal Safety Case for its " Scientist AI " . <h> News provided by <h> Share this article <p> Share toX <p> Share this article <p> Share toX <p> LawZero 's research team , led by Yoshua Bengio , makes the mathematical case for a " disinterested " AI that predicts the truth without pursuing goals of its own . <p> MONTR ? AL , July 2 , 2026 /CNW/ - LawZero , a nonprofit dedicated to safe-by-design artificial intelligence ( AI ) , today released a paper providing a new mathematical framework , representing a fundamental shift in the development of safe AI : one built to make honest predictions about the world without pursuing goals of its own . <p> Titled : " Safety from Honesty in a Disinterested AI Predictor " and authored by a team led by Yoshua Bengio , the work tackles what many researchers now consider a major danger of increasingly capable AI : that systems trained to imitate people and optimize for outcomes can quietly become goal-directed in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ AI systems learn first by imitating vast amounts of human-written text , and then by being rewarded for the answers approved by the users . <p> Today 's most powerful AI systems learn first by imitating vast amounts of human-written text , and then by being rewarded for the answers approved by the users . The paper argues that this training recipe can inadvertently incentivize systems to pursue unwanted goals of their own -- arising either from imitating human drives or wanting to maximize approval . This structural pressure can manifest as harmless-seeming flattery , or scale into highly critical safety risks such as deception or resistance to being shut down . The authors call this " implicit agency " : goal-seeking that no one asked for and that may not even be visible in the system 's stated answers . <p> " Most AI today is trained to act like us , to imitate , to please " , said Yoshua Bengio , Co-President and Scientific Director at LawZero . " We 're building something different : a system that mechanically applies the scientific method for hypothesizing and predicting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ honestly , including about what might harm us . Such a disinterested , scientist-like AI observes and analyzes rather than having hidden drives that can lead to scheming " , Bengio concluded . <p> A scientist , not an agent . <p> The proposed alternative is to build AI that behaves like a scientist reporting their best explanatory theories rather than act like an agent . A scientist tries to understand and predict the world accurately ; an agent tries to change it to get what it wants . LawZero 's " Scientist AI " predictor is trained only to estimate the probability of events through the most broadly explanatory hypotheses , and is given no incentive to influence what happens next as a consequence of its predictions , a property called consequence invariance . The paper calls this Scientist AI system disinterested ; it has no stake in the outcomes its predictions bring about . <p> Two design choices do the work . First , the system is taught to distinguish " someone claimed X is true " from " X is true " so it can learn from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ imitate it , i.e. , without absorbing human goals and biases as if they were established facts . <p> Second , and this is the heart of the safety case , the training process never rewards the system for the real-world consequences of its answers , only for the explanatory power of its hypotheses , avoiding the feedback loop that would otherwise teach it to manipulate . When the broader system needs to take actions , such as searching or using tools that work is handled by separate , auditable code with a safety guardrail that withholds any answer it judges to be too risky . <p> Why accuracy and safety reinforce each other . <p> The paper 's central result is a mathematical argument that , under clearly stated conditions , the chance of training such a system into a dangerous one is extremely small . Causing serious harm would require the system to be dishonest in a coordinated , sustained way across many separate answers -- yet the training method provides no push toward that , and the objective directly penalizes the kind of miscalibration it would demand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ another . The very honesty that makes the system useful is also what makes deception extremely unlikely , meaning there is no trade-off between accuracy and safety . <p> " The safety provided by the Scientist AI and its honest predictions makes it the ideal solution for monitoring and guard-railing frontier AI systems , " explained Iulian Serban , Senior Director , Research &amp; Development at LawZero . " By analyzing the actions , responses and history of other AI systems , the Scientist AI will more accurately and honestly evaluate whether their actions and responses may cause harm and , if so , block them . " <p> In addition to deploying the Scientist AI as a safety guardrail , LawZero expects the Scientist AI to act as a research acceleration tool providing hypothesis generation and probabilistic reasoning capabilities , helping researchers make new discoveries across fields ranging from medicine and climate change to cybersecurity and AI safety itself . <p> The authors are careful about scope , however : the paper 's argument addresses one specific risk ? the predictor itself developing hidden goals ? and is a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It does not by itself cover deliberate human misuse , one-off honest mistakes or the safety of larger , more capable agentic systems built on top of the predictor . However , agentic extensions are precisely the directions of current research at LawZero . The team presents the work as a foundation for safer AI and proposes concrete experiments to test its assumptions empirically . <p> Read the complete case . The full argument , including the formal proofs , the consequence-invariance result , and the experiments LawZero proposes to test it , is available here . <p> About LawZero <p> LawZero is a nonprofit organization committed to creating technical solutions that enable safe-by-design AI systems . Its scientific direction is based on new research and methods led by Professor Yoshua Bengio , the most cited AI researcher in the world . Based in Montr ? al , LawZero aims to build a safe-by-design AI that could be used to accelerate scientific discovery , to provide oversight for agentic AI systems , and to advance the understanding of AI risks and how to avoid them . The organisation aims @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ safely towards human flourishing . LawZero was incubated at Mila - Quebec AI Institute , a nonprofit academic research institution founded by Professor Bengio.

( Image Credit : submitted/SaskPolytech ) <p> Drone mapping is giving northern communities a faster and more detailed way to keep track of roads , homes , infrastructure and natural resources , with Montreal Lake Cree Nation among the latest communities taking part in the technology . <p> Researchers from Saskatchewan Polytechnic were in the community in June collecting aerial images as part of a three-year project that combines drone data , satellite imagery and local training . <p> Abdul Raous , Sask . Polytech 's research chair in geospatial technologies , said communities need maps that reflect constant changes as new homes , roads and other infrastructure are built . <p> " Maps are not static . They are dynamic , " Raous said . " They keep changing because we keep having new infrastructure , new houses and new roads . " <p> " The biggest advantage of drones is that you can choose the time , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there is no obstruction when we take those images . " <p> In Montreal Lake , researchers flew during the summer when longer daylight hours and snow-free conditions provided the clearest view of the community . <p> Raous said the team 's priority was documenting roads and recording the locations of community infrastructure , including homes and other buildings . <p> The information can be used to create digital maps that support community planning and improve emergency response , including meeting Next Generation 911 requirements by helping responders identify roads , buildings and other key assets . <p> The project also supports land and resource management . Researchers combine drone imagery with satellite data to map vegetation , water bodies and roads , while tracking changes caused by logging , wildfires and climate change . <p> Raous said satellites remain valuable because they cover large areas and provide historical imagery , while drones offer a much more detailed view of current conditions . <p> " The ultimate target is to help communities resolve whatever their issues are , " he said . " It could be environmental issues , mapping @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to develop a dashboard that allows communities to quickly identify features such as forested land , water , roads and infrastructure , including fire hydrants , power lines and power poles . <p> Training is another key part of the project . Raous said community members are learning how to maintain and update the mapping system after the grant-funded work concludes , ensuring the information remains current as communities continue to grow . <p> During the recent visit to Montreal Lake , Sask . Polytech also provided introductory drone training for interested residents , including information that could help them obtain drone licences and support future search-and-rescue efforts . <p> The project is funded through a federal grant , meaning partner communities do not pay for Saskatchewan Polytechnic 's mapping , training or technical support . <p> Raous said seeing the technology produce practical benefits for communities is one of the most rewarding parts of the work . <p> " You are helping communities , " he said . @@138622106 <h> The life of a pond -- Part II <p> Submitted photo . Wolfia spp. is an Indigenous species of duckweed that contains a number of rootless aquatic plants that are considered the smallest flowering plants on Earth . <p> Patricia Hanbidge <p> Orchid Horticulture <p> Last week , the focus was all about a catchment or retention pond ( Lake Omar ) that I overlook while I am working on Vancouver Island . This body of water is teeming with life and is an endless source of entertainment . What is even more amazing is what a catchment pond can do for the local environment . This pond has a function to hold rainfall run-off on a temporary basis . But actually , the work of these water bodies is so much more than that . A permanent retention pond , acts as a vital artificial ecosystem that provides significant environmental benefits . Water that is sustained throughout the year supports complex aquatic life and this biodiversity creates a thriving habitat oasis . <p> Last summer , we had an uncommon influx of aphids which particularly impacted the native @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was odd as I was reading about many other aphid infestations that were happening in many places . Most of these infestations were attributed to climate change with a slight increase in the overall mean temperature . Soon after the waterlilies had a dormant phase in early summer , I noticed a greening up on the pond . It was not algae but in fact duckweed that was rapidly turning the surface water green . There was the regular duckweed I have seen countless times , but it was the first time I had ever seen mealy duckweed . <p> Wolfia spp. is an Indigenous species of duckweed that first showed itself last summer on Lake Omar . This genus ( Wolfia ) contains a number of rootless aquatic plants that are considered the smallest flowering plants on Earth . They have a very cosmopolitan distribution so can be found in many nutrient-rich and still bodies of water . Each individual plant is a tiny , bright-green oval about the size of a grain of salt or cornmeal , giving it a unique texture . Students who were helping with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of May had the opportunity to view this tiny plant through a compound microscope . <p> The plant body of watermeal are entirely free-floating , branchless and lack both roots and true leaves . The consist of a simple , oval vegetative body called a thallus . They are technically a flowering plant , but the flower itself is quite unique . It has only one stamen and one pistil and forms in a tiny depression on the top of the plant 's frond . So the smallest flowering plants in the world are definitely not too showy ! <p> The ideal place for Wolfia to grow is warm water bathed in bright light . They reproduce exponentially via vegetative budding , and can double their population in just one or two days . Thriving in nutrient-rich freshwater environments , they form dense , green mats across the surface of lakes and ponds . There are almost a dozen species within the genus and I believe our major species in Lake Omar is Wolfia columbiana . This Indigenous species is an entirely spherical transparent- green plant . <p> This plant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and soy . It contains up to 40% protein by dry weight and is packed with essential amino acids , dietary fibre , vitamins and minerals . Cultivating this plan is incredibly environmentally friendly as it requires a fraction of the land and water that traditional crops demand . <p> Our world is experiencing global population growth and in emerging countries the demand for meat has triggered a " protein crisis " as the demand for protein has exceeded the supply . By 2030 , the imbalance between demand and supply is projected to become critical by 2030 . Our duckweed ( and other Wolfia species ) right here on Lake Omar could stand ready to solve this global crisis . This fast-growing crop is enjoying rising expectations as an alternative protein source to meat and soybeans . <p> In Hokkaido , Japan , the Floatmeal Company is a startup business in Japan 's largest food production region who are hoping to promote duckweed as a solution to the global protein crisis . The environmental impact of Wolfia is remarkably low using only 1/230 the water and 1/63 the land @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ high -- 36 to 40% compared with about 34% for soybeans and 28% for broccoli . Also rich in vitamins and minerals , wolfia could be the next focus of attention as a potential superfood to replace conventional protein sources . <p> Patricia Hanbidge is the Lead Horticulturist with Orchid Horticulture . Find us at www.orchidhort.com ; by email at growyourfuture@gmail.com on facebook @orchidhort and on instagram at #orchidhort . <p> Tune into GROW Live on our Facebook page or check out the Youtube channel GROW .

" <p> Since 2014 , he has served as Indigenous arts consultant to the Toronto District School Board and is currently both an Elder and artist-in-residence at the Urban Indigenous Education Centre , helping shape culturally informed curricula . @@138647637 <h> World 's oceans hit hottest June on record as marine heat waves intensify <p> The world 's oceans just experienced the hottest June on record and scientists believe the heat building beneath the surface may indicate more climate extremes ahead . <p> Global average sea surface temperatures reached 20.98 ? C in June , breaking previous records set in 2023 and 2024 , according to data released by the Copernicus Marine Service , the European Union 's ocean monitoring program . <p> The record is the latest warning sign in an already exceptionally warm year for the world 's oceans . <p> Scientists believe the concern extends beyond a single record-breaking month . Oceans absorb approximately 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions , making them one of the most reliable indicators of how quickly the climate is warming . <h> Heat building below the surface <p> Copernicus reported that the first half of 2026 was characterized by persistent ocean warmth and expanding marine heat waves . <p> Marine heat waves , which are prolonged periods of unusually high ocean temperatures , affected roughly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ six months of the year , the second-largest extent on record after 2024 . <p> Content continues below <p> That is significant as warmer oceans do not remain isolated at sea . <p> Hotter waters release more moisture into the atmosphere , increasing the likelihood of stronger storms , heavy rainfall and flooding . They also have a significant impact on marine ecosystems , particularly coral reefs , where prolonged heat can cause widespread bleaching and die-offs . <p> Scientists are monitoring the early stages of El Ni ? o , a climate pattern caused by unusually warm Pacific waters that can increase global temperatures . <p> " With ocean temperatures at these levels and El Ni ? o on the horizon , we are likely to see more temperature records fall in the coming months , " Carlo Buontempo , director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service , said in a statement . <h> Regional hot spots raise alarms <p> The Mediterranean Sea had its warmest June on record at 24.3 ? C , with marine heat waves affecting nearly the entire basin in the first half of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ record highs , potentially strengthening El Ni ? o conditions by 2026 . <p> Content continues below <p> Taken together , the regional data indicate a larger trend , ocean heat is not only persistent , but also becoming more sustained over longer periods of time . <p> That persistence has real-world implications . Warmer oceans can exacerbate storms , increase the risk of heavy rainfall and flooding and put additional strain on marine ecosystems that are already under threat from long-term warming . <p> Scientists warn that with summer still in full swing in many parts of the world , more records could be broken before the season ends .

Behind those numbers were millions of ordinary people forced to confront extraordinary times , as our world has become warmer . <h> ' It 's a reality I wish I 'd never seen ' <p> Dale Bass grew up in a Baptist Union family in southwestern Ontario . Her parents would n't pay for university , so she won the ' biggest and easiest scholarship ' she could find , funding four years that led , in 1976 , to a job reporting for the London Free Press , where she eventually headed the union @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moved to Kamloops when Alan assumed a professorship at Thompson Rivers University . On July 1 , 2021 , when the Juniper Ridge fire broke out in her city , just after Lytton burned , she was also grieving her son 's death . <p> This is Dale 's story as told to Sean Holman . <p> I did n't know it was on fire at all . And then our communications department sent out a press release saying , " Please stay off the highway . Juniper is being evacuated . There 's a fire coming . We have it all under control . Do n't panic , people . " That was the first I knew of that . <p> Then , a friend of mine who lives just east of Juniper called me in a panic because she saw a fire behind her house , which meant it had moved on down . I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ out a text to all of us saying , " I 'm in Juniper . I 'm stuck in this evacuation and we 're not going anywhere . " <p> There 's only one road in and out of Juniper , just one . It empties onto the highway , and it was just bogged down completely . Unloading everybody onto the Trans-Canada Highway led to all kinds of backups : people coming in or going out who were unaware of the fire , because they were backed up so far , were getting angry . <p> And I was hearing the horns honking because they did n't know the city was on fire . They just knew they were n't going anywhere and they were n't happy . There were n't even a lot of sirens . There were some . I guess that would 've been the police rushing to advise people they had to get out . I just remember sirens and horns . <p> There is a gate that is kept locked that leads to a dirt road that would 've been a great exit point @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . I had asked earlier , when we were discussing another matter at council , " Who 's got the key for that gate ? " " Fire Department does . " Fire department did n't have it . So somebody finally got bolt cutters and cut the damn lock . So , I was angry about that . <h> Surviving BC 's Hottest Summer <p> They are just lucky that they did n't lose any houses , and that was just from the work of the fire department . Because , like my house , they back up into the hills . The hills were on fire . There are trees , and there are bushes , a lot of sagebrush , and really , really expensive houses up there . @@138651723 <p> As New Yorkers prepare for one of the hottest Fourth of July weekends in years -- with temperatures of 100 ? F and heat indices exceeding 110 ? F -- public health officials warn of dehydration , heatstroke , and cardiovascular stress . Less appreciated is another danger : Extreme heat may increase the risk that a drug overdose becomes fatal . <p> For people using opioids , cocaine , methamphetamine , alcohol , or some prescription medications -- including diuretics , beta blockers , ACE inhibitors , antipsychotics , and antidepressants -- heat can do much more than cause discomfort . It can impair the ability to regulate body temperature , maintain hydration , and survive substance intoxication . Recent evidence shows extreme heat is an underrecognized risk factor for overdose and drug-related emergency visits and deaths , one likely to become increasingly important as climate change brings hotter summers and more frequent and extreme heat waves . <p> Several years ago , I argued that climate change could become an addiction medicine issue , not simply an environmental one . Rising temperatures , disrupted health care , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to converge and increase addiction-related illness and death . New research suggests this prediction is already becoming reality . <p> A national study led by Dr. Julia Dennett and colleagues at Yale University analyzed overdose deaths in nearly every U.S. county between 1999 and 2020 during the summer . Rather than examining air temperature alone , the researchers used the heat index , which combines temperature and humidity to better reflect the body 's physiological heat stress . <p> Their findings were striking . <p> Heat Makes Overdose More Deadly <p> Source : Mark Gold , MD with permission <p> Each 1 ? C increase in the heat index was associated with a measurable increase in overdose mortality , particularly deaths involving opioids , cocaine , and psychostimulants like methamphetamine . The investigators estimated that approximately 150 excess overdose deaths occur each year during periods of extreme heat . Applied across millions of people during increasingly frequent heat waves , the cumulative effect becomes a meaningful public health burden . <h> Cocaine-Hyperthermia <p> As a young cocaine researcher during the cocaine epidemic , I remember patients coming to the emergency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their drug use . Aggressive external cooling -- sometimes including ice-water immersion -- became standard emergency treatment because lowering body temperature was as important as treating the intoxication itself . The new Yale findings suggest environmental heat may produce a " second hit , " amplifying the toxic effects of opioids and stimulants and contributing to preventable overdose deaths . <p> Overdose has traditionally been viewed as a consequence of the drug itself -- its dose , potency , contaminants , or an individual 's underlying vulnerability . But extreme heat adds another risk factor . By placing additional strain on the cardiovascular , respiratory , and thermoregulatory systems , it reduces the body 's physiological reserve . <p> Under normal conditions , excess heat is dissipated through sweating and enhanced blood flow to the skin . High humidity , dehydration , many medications , and psychoactive drugs may impair these protective systems . As body temperature rises , the heart works harder , oxygen requirements increase , and dehydration further compromises circulation . A person who might survive drug intoxication under ordinary conditions may no longer be able to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ drug class . Stimulants -- including cocaine , methamphetamine , prescription amphetamines , and MDMA -- increase metabolic heat production , elevate heart rate and blood pressure , and impede the body 's ability to cool itself . Individuals may also increase their physical activity , but with reduced awareness of the effects of overheating . Hyperthermia can become part of the overdose syndrome itself , a phenomenon that emergency physicians have recognized for decades . <p> Opioids pose a different but equally dangerous threat . Respiratory depression remains the leading cause of fatal overdose , but heat magnifies the risk . Dehydration and cardiac stress reduce the body 's reserve , while fentanyl-induced respiratory depression limits oxygen delivery , just as heat increases metabolic demands . Together , these physiological stresses can turn a potentially survivable overdose into a fatal one . <p> Alcohol and some commonly-prescribed medications further raise vulnerability . Alcohol promotes dehydration and diminishes judgment , making it less likely someone will recognize heat illness or seek help . Certain antidepressants , antipsychotics , and medications with anticholinergic effects interfere with sweating , thirst , or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ substantially increase the risk of heat exhaustion , heatstroke , and overdose during periods of extreme heat . <h> Emerging Consensus <p> The Yale study is not an isolated finding . Researchers from California found hotter days were associated with increases in emergency department visits involving opioids , cocaine , and amphetamines . A Canadian study reported higher cocaine overdose mortality during periods of elevated ambient temperature . More recently , a systematic review concluded extreme heat consistently increases emergency health care utilization related to substance use disorders . Different drugs interact with heat through different biological pathways , but the overall conclusion has become increasingly consistent : heat magnifies overdose risks . <p> The Yale investigators also found the largest increases in overdose mortality occurred in people experiencing homelessness , unstable housing , poverty , limited access to air conditioning , or reduced access to health care . Many use drugs alone , making timely rescue less likely . Others avoid cooling centers because of stigma , untreated mental illness , or fear . In these settings , biological vulnerability and social vulnerability reinforce one another . <p> Public @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ children , and individuals with chronic medical illnesses to stay cool and hydrated . I think that people who use drugs should be considered another high-risk group . <p> Simple , evidence-informed interventions could save lives during periods of extreme heat . Expanding naloxone availability , establishing hydration and cooling stations , increasing outreach to people experiencing homelessness , reviewing medications that impair thermoregulation ( particularly psychotropic drugs ) , improving access to cooling centers , and encouraging people to avoid drug use during heat waves while connecting them with treatment are practical , relatively inexpensive measures . As extreme heat becomes more common , including these strategies in overdose prevention efforts should become standard public health practice , with costs that are small compared with the human and economic burden of preventable overdose deaths . <h> Prevention <p> Overdose prevention has traditionally focused on the drug , the dose , the route of administration ( oral , smoked , injected ) , and the individual . Emerging evidence now suggests a fifth factor deserves equal attention : the heat index and the environment . <p> Of course , extreme @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or alcohol as causes of overdoses . But it appears to magnify their lethality by reducing the body 's capacity to withstand them . 
@@138651731 <p> It is early July 2026 ; temperatures are above 90 ? F ( 32 degrees Celsius ) for several consecutive days . These daily interactions are an important and enjoyable part of her day . <p> Dina has loving family and friends who she sees when their schedules permit . But her walk is at her discretion and under her control , weather permitting . Walking keeps her fit , provides her with regular social connection , and maintains a connection to her community . For Dina , the park is far more than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lifelines . Her daily walk also helps protect her from loneliness and social isolation . At her age , walking outdoors in temperatures above 90 ? F poses significant health risks , leaving her with few safe alternatives . Although she has always been energetic and optimistic , the loss of her daily walks and the resulting isolation are beginning to affect her mood and well-being . <p> Dina 's experience is not unique . Although at 102 she is amazing , studies inform us that older adults of all ages walk for well-being and social connection . In fact , walking is the most popular form of physical activity in later life . As Dina 's case illustrates , climate-related heat can undermine not only physical activity , but also social connections @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more than 80% of older adults walk regularly , and even among adults aged 85 years and older , like Dina , more than 40% walk as their primary form of exercise . Walking is also inexpensive and accessible if safe walking spaces are available , which unfortunately is not always the case ( Tahmaseb McConatha , et al. , 2023 ) . Green spaces are not equally distributed ; poor older adults often lack a safe place to walk . For those who can , walking is a practical way for older adults to remain physically and socially active . For only 30 minutes , 5 times a week , physical and mental health can be improved . Research has long established that in addition to physical health benefits , walking promotes psychological well-being , social connection and engagement , as well as community participation . Even ten minutes of walking can improve mood , reduce stress , and enhance well-being . <p> In my ongoing work examining factors that promote well-being and protect against loneliness and social isolation in later life , walking has consistently emerged as one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to improving cardiovascular health , strength , and mobility , walking increases opportunities for social interaction , strengthens community connections , improves mood , and reduces the risk of anxiety and depression . Group walks , neighborhood strolls , and walks through parks and community spaces provide opportunities for natural , interpersonal , and social connections , making walking an important strategy for addressing loneliness and social isolation in later life . <p> The benefits of walking are even more crucial as loneliness and social isolation have emerged as a global public health crisis . The World Health Organization 's Commission on Social Connection ( 2025 ) reported that approximately one in six people worldwide experience loneliness , a condition that also contributes to an estimated 871,000 premature deaths annually . Loneliness and social isolation affect individuals across the life course , with younger adults being the loneliest , but older adults are particularly vulnerable given later life challenges that include role loss , such as retirement , loss of friends and family , chronic illness , mobility limitations , and living alone . <p> As social networks shrink , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Walking can increase social connections and boost positive emotions . Fredrickson 's ( 2001 ) broaden-and-build theory states that participation in meaningful and fulfilling activities such as walking increases positive emotions while helping individuals manage negative ones . The theory is useful in illustrating the ways that positive emotions can emerge from increased physical and social activity and as a result increase individual and social resilience . In my work , I have found that walking is a personally rewarding activity , in addition to the above-mentioned benefits , it also promotes a sense of control , and enhances meaning , purpose , and life satisfaction . <p> Walking in green spaces is particularly beneficial . Green spaces have the potential to provide a comforting environment , further fostering well-being . The many health benefits of connecting with natural spaces , forest bathing , and immersing oneself in nature are receiving considerable attention . Walking in parks and natural environments provides additional benefits for renewal , stress reduction , improving mood , and strengthening feelings of connectedness to nature . <p> Currently one of the greatest emerging threats to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to rise , extreme heat is becoming more common . On days when temperatures exceed 90 ? F , instead of promoting well-being , outdoor walking can become dangerous , even deadly . Extreme heat increases the likelihood of heat exhaustion , heat stroke , dehydration , and cardiovascular complications . Heat-related poor air quality present risks for those with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases . Warmer weather also leads to a larger number of mosquitoes and ticks , increasing exposure to infectious diseases such as Lyme disease . In such conditions , walking outdoors no longer promotes health but instead poses significant health risks . <p> There are widespread negative effects related to climate change . Adults of all ages report experiencing anxiety , grief , and uncertainty about environmental changes and the state of the planet . Eco anxiety ( Kurt &amp; Pihkala , 2022 ) is widespread and increases anxiety and depression in people of all ages and backgrounds ( Monsour et al. , 2022 ) . Although much of the research on eco-anxiety has focused on younger populations , older adults are vulnerable , particularly when the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ threat not only to their own well-being but that of future generations . <p> The effects of climate change are no longer abstract or distant . They are experienced daily . During the early summer days of 2026 , there have already been many days when heat and poor air quality have resulted in situations where older adults were advised to remain indoors , limiting opportunities for walking , exercise , and social interaction . For Dina and many others who depend on daily walks to maintain both physical health and social connection , repeated periods of extreme heat will increase sedentary behavior and lead to social isolation , and loneliness . For all of us , it is important to take steps to help combat climate change , to help increase the availability of accessible and safe walking spaces , to plant trees and shrubs when we can , and to recognize that all of our well-being depends on being able to walk outside .

This interview has been @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I was standing on the side of a road watching an incredible mirage of a site go by -- it was five or six gypsy wagons pulled by Clydesdale horses without riders , and goats , and kids and music . <p> And this vision just walked by at five miles an hour through Westworld , B.C. , where I was visiting my aunt . My mom , my siblings and I were moving up from the coast in ' 78 and finding shelter at my aunt 's place when this incredible vision went by . <p> It was paradigm shifting because I thought that kind of vision just exists in novels and fantasy books . To see something like that for a six-year-old kid who , you know , I loved novels and fantasy and creativity -- to see something like that just appear on the highway , stopping traffic , trundling along , really opened up a sense of possibility and magic that I 'm forever grateful for . <h> RELATED STORIES <p> What was that caravan doing at the time ? Photo for The Tyee by Jennifer Chrumka . <p> Can you fill in the gap between the trajectory of you as a child , having this profound experience , to then you becoming artistic director ? <p> I caught the theatre bug early on with the first productions I ever saw here . @@138699061 <h> Weather Alert <p> Take action to protect yourself and others -- extreme heat can affect everyone 's health . Determine if you or others around you are at greater risk of heat illness . Check on older adults , those living alone and other at-risk people in-person or on the phone multiple times a day . Watch for the early signs of heat exhaustion in yourself and others . Signs may include headache , nausea , dizziness , thirst , dark urine and intense fatigue . Stop your activity and drink water . Heat stroke is a medical emergency ! Call 9-1-1 or your emergency health provider if you , or someone around you , is showing signs of heat stroke which can include red and hot skin , dizziness , nausea , confusion and change in consciousness . While you wait for medical attention , try to cool the person by moving them to a cool place , removing extra clothing , applying cold water or ice packs around the body . Drink water often and before you feel thirsty to replace fluids . Close blinds , or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Turn on air conditioning , use a fan , or move to a cooler area of your living space . If your living space is hot , move to a cool public space such as a cooling centre , community centre , library or shaded park . Follow the advice of your region 's public health authority . Plan and schedule outdoor activities during the coolest parts of the day . Limit direct exposure to the sun and heat . Wear lightweight , light-coloured , loose-fitting clothing and a wide-brimmed hat . Never leave people , especially children , or pets inside a parked vehicle . @@138702578 <h> Dillon Alleyne Public policy and the quest for economic growth in Jamaica <p> Over the last three years , Jamaicans have withstood the devastating impact of Hurricanes Melissa and Beryl and tropical storm Raphael on the economy . These challenges raise an important question : How does public policy support growth in a small open economy ( SoE ) that is extremely vulnerable to external shocks and climate change ? <p> Any answer must confront a simple fact : the Jamaican economy has not grown significantly for at least two decades . Discounting shocks from the 2008-2010 financial crisis and COVID-19 , the story is one of anaemic growth . Between fiscal years 2010-11 and 2018-19 , growth varied between -0.7 per cent and 2 per cent and was 1 per cent or less for seven of nine years . After an 11 per cent decline during COVID , recovery rates between 2020-21 and 2022-23 merely reflected a very low base . Growth then returned to -0.5 per cent in 2023-24 and 0.5 per cent in 2024-25 . While Melissa 's full impact is unclear ( 56.7 per cent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ modest . <p> SOURCES OF GROWTH <p> Jamaica 's characteristics shape its growth path . It is a price taker : it can not set international prices but can export competitively at current ones , so binding constraints are mostly on the supply side . The economy supplies three types of goods : a traded export good consumed abroad ( largely tourism ) ; a non-traded good ( education , health , construction ) ; and imports of consumption and intermediate goods , with little short-run substitution . Because almost all production depends on imports , diversification is difficult . <p> Since Jamaica is a price taker , the key is improving product quality not lowering price . Exports earn the foreign exchange needed to buy essential imports , so foreign exchange is a binding constraint . Relaxing it provides resources for growth . These economies must , therefore , expand export capacity by raising productivity through innovation alongside non-traded improvements like logistics and labour productivity that complement exports . Public policy can build domestic capability in these areas . <p> Several implications follow : firms that use or save @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ carry heavy weight in the price index , inflation can not fall below that of Jamaica 's largest trading partner . Unsustainable fiscal deficits eventually drain foreign exchange , too , and when both crises converge ( fiscal and balance of payments ) , the economy grinds to a halt absent the IMF route . <p> There is a high correlation between attainable GDP per capita and three interactive forces : resources devoted to domestic capital production ( local capability ) , technology upgrading , and institutional strengthening . Successive governments have addressed the first and third through education , fiscal discipline , and bodies like an Independent Fiscal Commission , but is this enough ? Across 171 countries in 2019 , researchers found that every 1 per cent rise in per capita income accompanied 1.53 per cent export growth ( Hausmann 2025 ) . For Jamaica , between 1960 and 2024 , export growth was just 1.04 per cent . <p> The quality of exports matters as much as the level . With respect to goods , Jamaica exports primary and natural-resource-based products . In services , it remains @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ areas . Building domestic capability should yield more exports in health , education , and creative services . Production is constrained by low productivity and a poor ( though improving ) business environment , long aggravated by high crime . The global literature is clear : countries must export not only more existing products but new products to new markets , especially now given uncertainty from US trade policy . <p> DECLINING PRODUCTIVITY <p> Low growth is tied to declining productivity , hence the case for greater domestic capability . Despite falling unemployment , many workers remain in low-wage , low-productivity activities . Output per unit of labour fell roughly 19.1 per cent between 2004 and 2020 , with the decline intensifying after the 2008-2009 crisis . Total factor productivity ( TFP ) also fell between 2001 and 2019 . Economists usually refer to TFP as ' technology ' - a shift parameter that makes other factors more productive . Foreign exchange depends on too few sectors , reflecting weak diversification , the growth of tourism " enclaves " with limited spillovers , and an expanding low-productivity informal economy . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inefficient : gross fixed capital formation ( a measure of investment ) rose from 21 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 24 per cent in 2019 . <p> Years of fiscal stability have lowered the debt-to-GDP ratio and improved Jamaica 's risk profile . The question is how to spend the hard-won fiscal dividend . First , capital investment must prioritise building export capacity . The IFC notes that capacity constraints within ministries and agencies limit full use of the capital budget . What matters is not just spending but value for money . Second , Melissa underscores the need for adaptive expenditure . Each agency , public and private , must tag adaptive spending and assess effectiveness . Building resilience is a priority . Extreme events cost small island developing states an average 2 per cent of GDP annually - four times the rate for larger countries ( IMF , 2016 ) - while each dollar invested in adaptation yields four in benefits ( IDB ) . Resilience rests on financial protection ( insurance ) and structural protection ( adaptation investment ) , a trade-off to optimise with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of government at sourcing adaptation finance , a financing gap remains , and the private sector must be incentivised to help - best done through growth - or face higher taxes . <p> Jamaica can not reach 6-7 per cent growth on its current configuration , dependent on a few foreign-exchange sources led by tourism . Existing industries need not be abandoned but must serve as springboards . The country can not walk away from inherited structures . Instead , public policy , with the private sector , must create more value in existing sectors and search for new areas of competitiveness . It is not easy , but without it , growth will be far harder to sustain .

@@138723914 <p> Asim Biswas is a professor and Canada Research Chair in Digital Agriculture at the University of Guelph . <p> Canada has released its first National Food Security Strategy , and for a plan devoted to feeding the country , it has little to say about the ground in which that food is grown . <p> The strategy is needed , and overdue . Backed by more than $3-billion over 10 years , it sets out to loosen the grip of the five chains that control three-quarters of the grocery market , build food terminals and hubs , process more of what we grow at home , and expand year-round production under glass . The diagnosis is correct and the plan deserves credit for treating food as national resilience . <p> Yet one absence is striking : the word " soil " scarcely appears . There is a plan for the terminals , trucks , processing plants and greenhouses , and almost nothing for the thin layer of living topsoil that produces most of what Canadians eat . A food strategy built on everything but the soil is a house @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about where food dollars go . By its accounting , farmers receive about 11 cents of every dollar Canadians spend on food , processors 23 cents and retailers 16 cents . Ottawa reads those figures as a reason to invest downstream , and the logic is sound . But that 11 cents is n't just a cost to be cut with cheaper fertilizer ; it 's the soil 's productive capacity -- which we can build up or let erode . <p> The case for looking upstream is one the strategy itself makes . It cites the OECD 's estimate that climate change could reduce global corn yields by 16 per cent by mid-century and recalls the 2021 drought that cut Prairie wheat production by 37 per cent in a single year . Its main response is $750-million for greenhouses and vertical farms -- worthwhile , but limited . Greenhouses excel at cucumbers , tomatoes and peppers ; they do not produce the wheat , canola and pulses , the backbone of what Canada eats and exports . The most cost-effective insurance against the next drought is soil that holds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most of our calories are grown . <p> Fertilizer illustrates the point . The strategy notes that Canada imports roughly 35 per cent of its fertilizer , and that a quarter of the world 's traded nitrogen passes through one chokepoint , the Strait of Hormuz . The instinct is to secure more supply . The complementary , often faster measure , is to reduce demand : A farmer working healthy soil can grow the same crop with less imported nitrogen . Lowering what we need is itself a form of sovereignty . <p> The strategy 's most valuable opportunity is one the government has already created elsewhere . In March , the same Agriculture Minister , Heath MacDonald , committed Canada to a National Agricultural Soil Health Strategy , developed with the Soil Conservation Council of Canada and reinforced by Senator Robert Black 's Bill S-230 , the National Strategy for Soil Health Act . That bill , which has passed the Senate and now sits before the House of Commons , would recognize soil as a national asset essential to food security . Yet the food strategy barely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aimed at the same goal , advance on separate tracks . The single most useful revision would bind them , so the food strategy rests on the soil strategy , not beside it . <p> The clearest place to begin is data . The soil strategy already names improved data collection among its priorities . The food strategy 's organizing promise is " more choice , more control , more Canada , " yet control depends on measurement , and Canada estimates rather than measures how much carbon its farmland holds , whether that store is rising or falling , or which soils are most at risk . <p> We map our minerals and inventory our forests in detail , but we largely estimate the asset beneath the food system . A national soil-information system , modern digital soil mapping paired with credible measurement and verification , would turn " control " into something a farmer in Saskatchewan and a minister in Ottawa could act on . <p> None of this requires reopening the strategy . It requires connecting it to the soil work already under way , and funding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> A country 's capacity to feed itself rests on a thin layer of topsoil we have long treated as free and permanent . It is neither . The terminals and the greenhouses are worth building . But a food-security strategy that omits the soil has overlooked the one thing on which all the rest depends .

@@138771675 <p> Tornadoes , floods , wildfires and storms have all been in the news recently , and all are taken as harbingers of a coming climate catastrophe . The word " unprecedented " is often used in such reports , but are these disruptive weather events unusual for the various climates of Canada ? How can we tell ? It feels as if we are adrift in a sea of events , statistics and crises , with no anchors or waypoints . <p> As with many disciplines , we climatologists turn to history to stabilize ourselves in a constantly churning sea of change . Flood markers and rain gauges date back millennia , while modern thermometers and barometers were invented near the middle of the 17th century . People have been recording weather and climate ever since , leaving us with several centuries of historical weather diaries and climatic records . <p> In Canada , the earliest instrumental records date to the first half of the 18th century , with recordings from Hudson Bay in the 1730s and Qu ? bec City in the 1740s . We have records stretching @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gain insights on an incredible scale , over both time and space . When we can access the original documents , we can look at weather recordings taken at intervals of only a few hours . This means we can track everything from intense but brief events , such as sudden downpours leading to flash flooding , to the slow variability and change that occurs over centuries . <p> In 2020 , colleagues and I started a not-for-profit called Open Data Rescue , with a mandate to locate , transcribe and analyze these historical weather and climate records . <p> With support from Environment and Climate Change Canada , we found records of Canadian weather and climate from 50 locations in archival sources outside of Canada , mainly from the National Archives and Records Administration and National Centre for Environmental Information in the United States and the Meteorological Office Library and Archives in the United Kingdom . <h> Our research <p> We faced a host of challenges transcribing 18th- and 19th-century weather records and using them for climate analysis . For one thing , many of the records kept in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Smithsonian Institution in Washington , D.C. as monthly registers . <p> One can only imagine the journey they must have gone through via canoe or dog sleds from , say , Fort Rae on Great Slave Lake to York Factory on the western coast of Hudson 's Bay , and then to Washington . The documents are appropriately tattered , torn and ink-smudged , making it difficult if not impossible to recover the original text . <p> Other times the observations or units are hard to convert . Before reliable anemometers were developed , wind speed was measured in a variety of ways , mostly using wind force scales derived from environmental conditions such as leaves rustling , trees swaying , smoke blowing from chimneys and other such cues such as the Beaufort wind scale . <p> The Royal Engineers , being engineers , recorded the wind force in pounds per square inch , using pounds and ounces . Converting all these to metres per second required considerable research . <p> Our analysis of sub-daily weather records in the St. Lawrence Valley region led to the counter-intuitive conclusion that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ distinct warming trend in the coldest winter temperatures -- it 's not clear that it 's getting warmer during the daytime in summer in southwestern Qu ? bec than in the past . <p> Even as we experience heat domes and higher temperatures , descriptions of past hot summers , severe droughts , heatwaves and fire resonate today . Looking beyond headlines , we may need to concentrate as much on the impacts of warmer winters , such as repeated freeze-thaws leading to icy surfaces and increased accidents , as we do on heatwaves as our climate continues to change . <h> The 1826 Red River flood <p> Flooding is another challenge that has always been present . The 1826 flooding of the Red River in what is now Manitoba was catastrophic . Coming at the end of two years of poor harvests , an already stressed and even starving population had to contend with what was likely one of the biggest floods of the past 500 years . <p> This led to the relocation of the Hudson 's Bay Company headquarters from Upper Fort Garry in present-day Winnipeg to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Flood defences were built around the city after subsequent 19th-century floods , helping mitigate future catastrophes . <p> It is somewhat reassuring that many of the events we 're facing now have been faced in past by our predecessors , who had far fewer resources at hand . It may be that we will need to undo some of their work order to find a better balance between our desire to control our environment and the inevitable facts of living on an active planet . <p> Restoring wetlands in place of concrete flood defences is an example that comes to mind . We have been adaptable and resilient in the past . @@138785097 <p> Scientists are often told that admitting uncertainty is a mistake . In a world where confident misinformation spreads quickly , it can feel like the safest strategy is to sound certain , simplify the message , and avoid highlighting what we do n't yet know . <p> But that instinct may be backwards . <p> A 2026 literature review found that transparency about scientific uncertainty generally builds trust rather than eroding it . Downplaying or concealing uncertainty tends to foster distrust , especially over the long term . The fear that admitting uncertainty backfires is mostly unsupported . <p> That does n't mean uncertainty communication is simple or risk-free . It means the risks are different than many people assume , and they depend heavily on how you do it . Let 's dive into some specifics : <h> How you express uncertainty matters <p> First off , not all uncertainty language lands the same way , and the words you use to describe uncertainty can make a big difference . <p> A series of studies investigated how different types of uncertainty language affect trust . The clearest finding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and 1,555,000 " ) communicate uncertainty while barely reducing trust . Vague verbal hedges ( " it could be somewhat higher or lower " ) register as uncertainty too , but they cost more trust . And weak words like " estimated " often do n't even register as uncertainty to most people at all . <p> Practical takeaway : if you have a range , give the range . Do n't round it off into a mushy qualifier or vague hedging . <h> Disclose early -- it protects trust later <p> Here 's a useful finding for anyone communicating science , but especially if they do science that can be rather fast-moving . This study examined how communicating uncertainty about vaccines affected trust . The researchers found that when evidence is later reversed , trust drops less if uncertainty was flagged up front . Simply stating " this may change " is enough to buffer the loss . <p> Disclosing uncertainty early makes future updates feel like science working as intended , not science failing . <p> This is the opposite of how a lot of institutions communicate during @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ things right away , because certainty feels reassuring in the moment . But that certainty is like a loan against future trust , and the interest rate is high . <h> An audience 's prior beliefs shape the effect <p> Uncertainty communication does n't hit everyone the same way , as prior beliefs do matter . A 2025 study found that when evidence matches what someone already believes , adding uncertainty slightly lowers trust . However , when evidence contradicts people 's prior beliefs , communicating uncertainty actually increases trust . The researchers focused on vaccination and climate change because these issues have well-defined groups of believers and skeptics , making it easier to see how prior beliefs shaped people 's responses . <p> What I found most interesting was the overall pattern . Even on highly polarized issues , there was a kind of balancing effect . Communicating uncertainty caused trust to converge across the belief spectrum . <p> In other words , honest uncertainty does n't just preserve trust on average . With polarized topics , it can actually narrow the gap between people who started out skeptical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ process , not just the doubt <p> It 's not enough to simply acknowledge uncertainty . Research shows that public health communication is more trustworthy when uncertainty is explained with compassion , its causes are made clear , it is presented as a normal part of science , and people are told when to expect updates . <p> But there 's a ceiling on what any single message can do . This study also found that prior trust in institutions was the strongest predictor of how a public health message landed . No single message undoes years of eroded trust . <p> This is an important caveat , and I 'll share a few more at the end of this post . Good communication technique matters , but it 's operating within limits set by history . A perfectly worded message from a distrusted source will still struggle . <h> Genuine vs. manufactured uncertainty <p> So far , these communication strategies have focused on how to build trust , but this study found how you can quickly undermine it . Uncertainty language applied to settled science can manufacture doubt and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2025 CDC vaccine-autism webpage revision provided us with a real-world case study that could be evaluated . The new CDC under RFK Jr . changed language from " there is no link " between vaccine and autism to " studies have not ruled out the possibility . " This study , recently published in Science , tested how people felt about that change in communication , and found that it raised perceived vaccine risk , lowered vaccination intentions , reduced CDC trust , and increased science-denial reasoning ( across the political spectrum ) . <p> Notably , the damage was institution-specific . It hit trust in the CDC , not a blanket loss of trust in scientists generally . <p> While disclosing genuine uncertainty can build trust , manufacturing doubt about settled science does the opposite . The damage does n't stay contained to the specific claim as it can bleed into trust in the institution itself . <h> The structural caveats <p> Of course , none of this works in a vacuum , and it 's worth being honest about the limits of simply improving our communication . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ single message undoes years of eroded trust or a hostile information environment . Science communicators need real support , but right now we ask researchers and clinicians to address falsehoods with no training , no time , and little institutional backing . <p> The incentives also run the wrong way . Algorithms reward certainty and outrage . Careful , hedged , accurate communication is at a systemic disadvantage before it even reaches an audience . <p> And AI and disinformation ca n't be ignored . Generative AI produces confident falsehoods at scale , and it exploits the same identity dynamics that make uncertainty hard to communicate in the first place . <p> The fix has to be systemic , not just individual . We need to support the messengers of science and also change the structures . <h> The bottom line <p> Transparency about genuine uncertainty , communicated thoughtfully and with attention to audience , can build trust . <p> For specific tips : Use concrete numbers/ranges when appropriate over vague hedges . Disclose early . Explain why the uncertainty exists . Normalize it as part of how science works @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ audience already believes . <p> Feel free to disclose what you do n't know . Just do n't manufacture doubt about what you do .

Peachland does n't have a water problem , right ? There 's a vast watershed above the town and a lake 160 kilometres long at our feet , right ? <p> Only two years ago , a District-commissioned report by Urban Systems pegged population growth , not climate change , as the biggest water challenge facing Peachland . Annual reservoir shortfalls driven by climate change " are expected by the 2060s , " said the April 2024 report called Peachland Water Creek Supply Under Future Climate Assessment . <p> But the current drought appears to be turning that timeline upside down . And District council and staff are paying attention to discussions in Peachland about the town 's ability to provide treated water to residents now , let alone as the town grows . <p> ARTICLE @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from Peachland Creek , which is fed by Peachland Lake , which dropped to critically low levels this year after several years of drought . @@138846667 <p> Annual gatherings of the great democracies in the age of Donald Trump have acquired a certain ... rhythm . There is the meeting that takes place before the President arrives , when all is as it usually is between world leaders of the same broad ideological hue : convivial open sessions , chummy photo-ops , urgent side-conferences . <p> Then there is what happens after he gets there , and the desperate scramble to reconcile the chaos that ensues with the serene normalcy that went before : to insist that the torrent of lunacies foaming out of the President 's mouth from the moment of his arrival , making hash of everything the other conferees had agreed upon -- not to mention decades of settled international law -- were in fact in perfect harmony with the rest . <p> This year 's NATO summit in Ankara , Turkey , was no different . The meeting had been intended to be a carefully staged show of support for Ukraine in the war with Russia , coupled with an equally carefully staged display of Europe 's commitment to its own defence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that the bargain struck at NATO 's 2025 meeting in The Hague -- higher non-U.S . defence spending in return for continued U.S. engagement in Europe -- was actually being implemented . <p> Then Mr. Trump arrived . He had been attacking and ridiculing NATO , and individual NATO leaders , for months prior to the summit , particularly over their failure to involve themselves in the Iran war -- a debacle that has nothing to do with NATO or its core mandate . At the summit things escalated . Mr. Trump revived his demands to be given Greenland , called for a boycott on trade with Spain , and threatened to withdraw all U.S. troops from Europe , on his way to redeclaring war on Iran . <p> But by the time it was over all was supposedly sweetness and light . The post-conference declaration insisted on the alliance members ' " ironclad " commitment to defend each other under Article 5 of NATO 's founding treaty , mentioned " the long-term threat Russia poses , " boasted that European allies and Canada had increased spending on core defence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' " unwavering support for Ukraine . " <p> Mr. Trump , for his part , seemed pleased , not least by the flattery the other leaders laid on him , which he interpreted as love . " They said , ' We love , sir , we love you . ' These are grown people saying that , is n't that nice ? ... I 've never seen anything like it . Every one of those countries , they love us , they love each other . " Whatever it was , it seemed to work . Mr. Trump even promised to license Ukraine to make U.S. Patriot air defence systems . <p> Of course , at most NATO summits , it would not be news that Article 5 was still intact , that the U.S. was still in it , or that the alliance viewed Russia as a threat . But that was before Mr. Trump came onto the world scene . The meeting might have succeeded in papering over the deep cracks in the alliance , but no one takes seriously Mr. Trump 's commitments , such @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not what NATO partners say about it now , but what they do in the event of an attack . <p> Prime Minister Mark Carney says President Donald Trump arrived at NATO in a good mood and the alliance is shifting military budget burdens away from the U.S. <p> The Canadian Press <p> To say that there is now profound doubt about the United States ' willingness to defend its allies is to understate things considerably . To say that there is almost complete certainty in NATO circles that it would not is still to understate matters . The most recent , and serious , threat to the territorial integrity of a NATO member , after all , did not come from Russia . It came , and comes , from the United States : over Greenland . And it lingers still over Canada . <p> The Wall Street Journal this week revived controversy over a conversation first reported last year , in which Mr. Trump had allegedly threatened , in a phone call with Prime Minister Justin Trudeau , to abrogate the Treaty of 1908 , defining the border @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that up and your whole country unravels , " Mr. Trump reportedly told Mr. Trudeau . <p> However much Mr. Trump 's belligerence may have changed relations with the rest of NATO , it is nothing compared to how it has transformed relations with Canada -- and changed Canada with it . Never , since 1867 , have we had to take seriously the prospect that the President of the United States might attempt to seize a part of our territory , by one means or another . <p> Quite the opposite . The United States became our benefactor : our largest trading partner , closest ally , and military protector . No major democracy is more dependent on another country for trade , nor does any other depend as much on another for its defence . <p> That Canada combines both is a measure not just of how much we had come to rely on the United States , but how uniquely ill-prepared we are for the world we are now in -- a world in which we not only can not rely on the United States for our @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> U.S. President Donald Trump and Mr. Carney attend a meeting of the North Atlantic Council during the NATO leaders ' summit.Yves Herman/Reuters <p> And yet , it must be said , there are opportunities for Canada in this world . Sheltering within the U.S. trade and defence orbit had many benefits -- assured access to U.S. markets , security from external aggression -- but also infantilized us in many ways . <p> It convinced us , not only that we did not have to pay for our own defence , but that we had no need to defend ourselves -- that we had no natural predators . It dulled our competitive edge , leading us to neglect our sputtering productivity -- why concern ourselves with such things , when we could always ship our commodities south ? <p> It allowed us to indulge in self-destructive behaviour like imposing hundreds of interprovincial trade barriers on ourselves , or indulging periodic threats of secession from one province or another . It permitted us to rely on tenuous east-west transportation and communications links that left us more vulnerable than we might @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ threat of sabotage or other coercive measures . <p> And it encouraged us in that most Canadian of pastimes , preaching to others about matters that do not directly concern us , based on claims to superior virtue we have not earned -- a particular irritant when it came to our notorious NATO freeloading , but a tendency to preen that had more generally consigned us to the sidelines of international affairs . <p> All of this is about to change -- is changing already . We have been forced to change course on any number of fronts at the same time , the most radical reappraisal of our prospects and direction in at least the last 40 years , maybe since 1945 -- maybe ever . <p> At one go , we are attempting to redirect some of our trade to other nations besides the U.S. , including by a series of sweeping free trade agreements , while raising our defence spending to levels , whether in proportion to our GDP or to total government spending , not seen since the early 1960s . <p> At the same time @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ again of a kind not seen in decades : pipelines and electricity links and railways and more . Rather less has been done as yet on the productivity or internal trade barriers fronts , but these will surely have to follow -- there is no way we will be able to pay for all this other spending if we do n't . <p> And we are beginning to be taken seriously again in international councils . Mark Carney 's personal reputation , as a former central banker and international financier , is only part of this . The reason his speech at Davos , calling on middle powers to get out from under the " hegemons ' " thumbs , landed with such enormous impact was not just who said it , or where , or when -- at the height of the Greenland fiasco -- but that it was a Prime Minister of Canada , of all places , saying it . <p> This was n't Canada preaching from the sidelines . This was a politician with skin in the game , leading a country that was more dependent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there -- and therefore more at risk . As a consequence , we are taking an outsized role in the construction of a post-American world . <p> Perhaps the most startling , and sudden , transformation has been our approach to energy development . The Prime Minister 's remarkable " forward guidance " video the other day amounted to a blunt disavowal of the last 10 years of Liberal policy . His reasoning was simple . The world has changed . New threats crowd upon us , that were not anticipated a decade ago , and new priorities must take their place alongside the fight against climate change . Government is about triage . <p> But it is n't only Justin Trudeau 's legacy Mr. Carney has been busy overturning , for good or ill . It 's Pierre Trudeau 's . Mr. Carney is in many ways a throwback to a pre-Trudeau kind of Liberal . In style and tone , but even more in policy , he recalls the Liberals of the Lester Pearson era , and even more that of Louis St. Laurent : sober , bankerly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Pearson as the father of peacekeeping . We are less likely to remember him as the Cold Warrior who accepted nuclear missiles on Canadian soil , and who spent more than 3 per cent of GDP , on average , on defence . <p> It was the Diefenbaker Conservatives who objected to the missiles . At the time the Liberals were the continentalists of Canadian politics , seeing engagement with the U.S. as a necessary counterbalance to the imperial connection they were so anxious to be rid of . The Tories were the opposite : fond of the mother country , suspicious of the Yanks . Only much later did the roles reverse , after Britain ceased to be an issue . <p> Mr. Carney is a continentalist , too -- he just has a different continent in mind . But his ardent pursuit of the European connection is in the same counter-balancing mould , not only of Liberal leaders past , but of statesmen through the ages : calling the Old World back into our existence , to redress the balance of the New .
