@@138847310 <p> Benjamin Laker , Ph.D. , is a professor of leadership at Henley Business School , University of Reading . His research evaluates the societal impact of leadership , often influencing government policies and law . He introduced and subsequently popularized the concept of Meeting-Free Days : a method used by organizations to optimize employees ' productivity through strategic avoidance of non-essential meetings . Since its introduction , Meeting-Free Days has been adopted by many organizations across the globe , including Facebook , Microsoft , SAP and Shopify . Benjamin is often asked to attend United Nations Climate Change Conferences and United States House Select Committee hearings that supply public policy recommendations to the United States Congress . His proximity to lawmaking effectuates regular interviews with BBC News , Bloomberg , CNBC , Financial Times , The New York Times , The Wall Street Journal , The Washington Post , and USA Today . 
@@138847321 <p> Slightly modifying our lifestyles by allowing more quiet time , rest time , and emotional honesty is key . <p> Individual engagement drives collective action . <p> This summer , England 's temperatures reached 99.9 degrees Fahrenheit , the highest June temperature on record in the UK . A heat wave triggered a " red heat health alert " at exactly the same time the city of London was hosting its 8th annual Climate Week . The irony here is obvious . <p> The British experienced cascading climate disruptions -- nature 's reminders to wake the heck up . The sweltering temperatures cut off vital transportation services , closed schools and businesses , and caused hospitals to restrict services as they struggled to cope with an influx of heat-related demands . <p> Beneath the immediate chaos , an urgent question looms : Can the British look up , notice , and care -- even after these hot days finally pass ? Can any of us ? <p> As a psychotherapist working at the intersection of climate and mental health , I spend a good deal of time tracking emotional @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A new Yale Program on Climate Change Communication ( YPCCC ) poll reveals that a solid majority of Americans ( 65% ) say that global warming is personally important to them . Yet , there is a high level of cognitive dissonance ( or conflicting thoughts , feelings , and behaviors ) as people struggle to reconcile fears , worries , grief , and hopes with ordinary life . <p> What I see happening in England , and many other countries , is something the YPCCC has called the " attitude-behavior gap . " This is the fancy term for the very real discrepancy between human concern and climate action engagement . As YPCCC research indicates , even amongst those most willing to act ( 51% ) , few actually engage in political actions to limit global warming ( 6-16% ) , such as contacting government officials , attending protests , and signing petitions . This attitude-behavior gap is deeply problematic because human behavior tilts towards complacency at a time when climate collapse is accelerating . <p> What if we could harness the collective energy of the 89% global majority @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ effectively intensify collective pressure on world governments , institutions and businesses ? <p> Here in the U.S. , America 's natural resources -- including air , water , and public lands -- are in jeopardy under the Trump administration , which has rolled back environmental protections and clean energy investments . This is precisely the moment that human concern for the environment and human health ought to be vocalized ( ad nauseam ) to build public pressure demanding government response . <p> In my clinical work , I 've found that giving folks language for understanding the psychological mechanisms and structural barriers they encounter when it comes to the climate crisis is a helpful way of unsticking their psyches . Although there are many such barriers , a few key ones worth noting are : Noise , Depletion , and Intellectualization . <h> Noise <p> Noise is a catch-all for busy people leading busy lives -- and/or oppressed and marginalized people leading oppressed and marginalized lives . Our busy-ness is no accident -- it 's by design . The inherent expectations of capitalism -- efficiency , productivity , economic growth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ us . Capitalism , as right-wing strategist Steve Bannon has identified , is an effective engine for breeding collective complacency ( " flood the zone with sh*t ) . " <p> If we 're honest with ourselves , can we admit that it 's easy to be lulled into a state of submission , or remain frozen , or numb , entranced by a Pied-Piper-like spell that tells us to " keep looking away " rather than face the existential elephant in the room ? <p> Just because people are distracted by noise does not mean that they do n't care about climate change . People tend to assume that others around them do n't care about the climate crisis , but this simply is n't true . A " perception gap " exists in which people tend to underestimate their fellow citizens ' concern for the environment . In fact , polls consistently show that the majority of the global population does , indeed , want climate action and would even make personal sacrifices to help . <p> Additionally , a large segment of folks who care deeply about @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and eking out survival to have space or bandwidth to engage . The cost of living crisis suppresses the ability to act . In the U.S. , notoriously sparse family-friendly policies ( e.g. paid maternity/paternity leave , affordable healthcare and childcare ) mean that that less resourced folks are overburdened with day to day concerns . Meanwhile , the middle class is kept saturated and distracted by a culture of consumerism . For those of us who are able to cut through this Noise , it is our responsibility to act . <h> Depletion <p> Depletion is a physical and emotional state of " running on empty " that stems from ambient Noise . It turns out that , eventually , living with constant over-stimulation and too little rest catches up with you . Long workdays . Second or third jobs . Cost-of-living struggles . Intense careers that do n't allow you to clock out at the end of a long day . And , of course , the glaze-eyed exhaustion from the most demanding relationship of all -- your smartphone . <p> The pings . The posts . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ demand our constant attention from the moment we wake up to the moment we go to sleep . A pervasive cloud hangs over our heads of " I just ca n't keep up " that leaves us feeling ragged at the end of each day . Burnout , at least in the US , is difficult to avoid . <p> Living in a depleted state is not healthy for anyone , including children , nor will it help tackle our climate crisis . To stay depleted means kicking the existential can further and further down the street -- rather than picking it up ourselves . A depleted society is not in any shape to look after its future generations . <h> Intellectualization <p> Perhaps the most subtle barrier to climate engagement is Intellectualization -- an interesting form of mental gymnastics subconsciously adopted to insulate people from the emotional pain of the climate crisis . On one hand , people are honest about the hard realities of the climate crisis , but on the other , climate emotions are kept at arm 's length . When we shield ourselves from pain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we deny the emotional gravity of the situation . Yet , emotions are actually portals to motivation , care and engagement . By keeping those doors shut , we pay a price . <p> These are only three barriers to climate engagement . But keep in mind that Noise , Depletion , and Intellectualization are temporary traps . With intention , we can move past them and carve a path forward that will be meaningful , productive , and clarifying . This is the hope of climate behavioral change . <h> Simple Solutions <p> To combat noise , seek quiet . Try to spend time in quiet spaces -- like libraries , book stores , museums , parks , forests , beaches or public gardens . Create a quiet zone in your home -- for example , a porch , a seat near a window , a corner of a room that is discussed and agreed upon -- or use a pair of noise-canceling headphones . Perhaps you set up some comfy pillows or put a sign up on the wall to designate a quiet space . If you live @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hours each day ( e.g. , early morning , before bedtime ) . Consider making this quiet time device-free as well . <p> Building Quiet time back into our lives reminds us to slow down , reconnect with our thoughts and feelings , and to replenish ourselves . One of my clients starts each morning on his balcony with tea , another unwinds on her rooftop at the end of the day , watching the sunset . Granting our brains some breathing room will help us to internally settle and regroup , so that we stay connected to ourselves , and our values and priorities . And it keeps us sane , too . <p> To combat depletion , try replenishment . Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith has identified 7 types of rest that every person needs ( and it involves more than kicking your feet up at the end of the day ) . Yes , she mentions physical rest and mental rest . But she goes further , including sensory rest ( i.e. , shutting out overwhelming stimuli ) , emotional rest ( i.e. , honestly expressing your feelings ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ relationships ) , and spiritual rest ( i.e. , connecting to something larger than yourself ) . If ever there were a prescription for our current existential woes , it is this ! We ca n't tackle climate change if we are not reasonably well-rested . <p> To combat Intellectualization , try emotional composting in your community or with a buddy or professional . We spend a lot of time avoiding our feelings because we 're afraid of them and worry that they will consume us . In fact , it 's just the opposite : our avoidant tendencies drive up inner tension and distress . The only way to experience relief is by honestly sharing our feelings . When we share our feelings with others , it 's even more beneficial because we discover that we are not alone , and we can feel validated , and even motivated by one another . Emotional composting is a process of breaking down messy complex emotions into identifiable ones so that we move towards greater emotional attunement . From there , it 's easier to act . <p> In order to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ waves , triggers extreme weather events and pushes us past dangerous planetary tipping points , then we must activate our quiet attention , we must find ways to replenish ourselves physically , emotionally and spiritually , and we must sit with our emotions in an honest way . This is a basic global prescription , regardless of where you are located . <p> When we understand the forces that keep us from acting -- Noise ! Depletion ! Intellectualization ! -- we can stop running in the same tired , predictable circles that perpetuate avoidance . And we can collectively address the climate crisis rather than leave it up to climate activists , professionals , and frontline communities . Our planet and younger generations desperately need us to wake up , stay vigilant , and act in alignment with our eco-concern . Now , more than ever . As humans , we have the power to modify our behaviors -- and we can start today .

@@138893454 <p> Picture this : a colossal structure , intricately woven from branches , twigs , and mud , stretching across the landscape as far as the eye can see . It 's not a man-made wonder like the Great Wall of China or the Pyramids of Egypt , but rather a creation of one of nature 's most ingenious engineers -- the beaver . Nestled in Wood Buffalo National Park in Alberta , Canada , lies the world 's largest beaver dam , an awe-inspiring feat that is so massive it can be seen from space . Yes , you read that right ! Let 's delve into the fascinating world of the beaver and discover the astonishing story behind this extraordinary creation . Wood Buffalo National Park is a vast wilderness that straddles the Alberta-Northwest Territories border . Covering an area larger than Switzerland , it is home to a diverse range of flora and fauna , including the iconic beaver . Beavers are renowned for their ability to transform landscapes by constructing dams and lodges . These industrious creatures have been shaping the environment for thousands of years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ beaver dam in Wood Buffalo National Park , known as the " Lac St. Clair Beaver Dam , " is a true testament to the beavers ' determination and ingenuity . Spanning an incredible length of approximately 850 meters ( 2,790 feet ) , it is the largest beaver dam ever recorded . To put that into perspective , it 's almost three times the length of the Empire State Building ! So , how did these furry engineers manage to create such an enormous structure ? Well , it all starts with their innate instinct to build and maintain a suitable habitat . Beavers construct dams across rivers and streams to create deep ponds that provide protection from predators and serve as a reliable food source during the winter months when water bodies freeze over . Using their sharp teeth , beavers fell trees and gather branches , which they meticulously interweave with mud and stones to form the dam . The resulting structure is incredibly sturdy and resistant to erosion . Over time , the dam grows as the beavers continuously reinforce and expand it , creating a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Dam is so immense that it was actually discovered via satellite images . " Scientists were examining thousands of satellite images searching for the effects of melting permafrost and landscape changes that result from climate change . They found the beaver dam by coincidence during this work , noticing its very large and distinctive horseshoe-shaped shoreline , " said the Government of Canada 's Website . Wood Buffalo National Park , recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site , serves as a vital refuge for countless species , and the beaver dam plays a crucial role in its ecosystem . The dam acts as a natural water regulator , controlling water flow and preventing flooding during periods of heavy rainfall . It also creates a rich wetland habitat that supports an array of plants , insects , birds , and mammals . Wood Buffalo National Park offers visitors a unique opportunity to witness the beaver 's impressive handiwork up close . Exploring the park 's wetlands and waterways , you can observe the beavers diligently building and maintaining their dams , an experience that truly showcases the wonders of nature @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and a contributor to Great West Media . @@138900211 <h> New research traces how ' forever chemicals ' move through the Great Lakes and into people <h> Share this article <p> The researchers analyzed 42 years of studies and combined nearly 2,500 samples of algae , fish , birds and other organisms , in what 's called a meta-analysis to identify trends in PFAS distribution . Photo by : Getty Images via Grist <p> This story was originally published by Grist and appears here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration . This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and Interlochen Public Radio in northern Michigan . ? ? <p> In the United States , PFAS chemicals are so ubiquitous -- found in everything from frying pans to skincare -- that nearly all of the country 's population likely has measurable levels of the so-called " forever chemicals " in their blood . It 's only in the last few decades that the public and scientists started untangling the health and ecological risks associated with some of the manufactured compounds , which earned their nickname because they do n't break down easily in the environment . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Dame has deepened our understanding of how PFAS can filter through ecosystems and move up the food chain to get to people . <p> The peer-reviewed study , published this spring in the Journal of Environmental Quality , focused on the Great Lakes . The researchers analyzed 42 years of studies and combined nearly 2,500 samples of algae , fish , birds , and other organisms , in what 's called a meta-analysis to identify trends in PFAS distribution . <p> PFAS have been linked to a range of health issues and the chemicals have been identified in human tissue , including in the bloodstream , liver , kidneys and lungs . Known health risks range from decreased fertility to a higher prevalence of certain cancers . People can be exposed to PFAS in several ways , including through the food they eat . <p> " What we 're finding is that the food web itself is a vehicle for transferring these chemicals from one organism to another , " said Gary Lamberti , aquatic science professor at Notre Dame and a study co-author . " So it 's a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The Great Lakes study focused on six of the PFAS chemicals most commonly tested for , but there are more than 15,000 types out there , according to the National Institutes of Health . Researchers identified a dramatic decrease over the last two decades of one PFAS chemical known as PFOS , following a voluntary phaseout by industries in the early 2000s . <p> " If we stop manufacturing these chemicals , they will eventually reduce in concentration in the food web , " Lamberti said . " That 's kind of good news for how we can manage these chemicals . " <p> Those declines were seen in the lower Great Lakes -- Ontario and Erie -- likely because these areas are home to the heavy industries that used the chemicals . <p> But there was little to no decline in PFOS in the upper lakes Superior , Michigan and Huron , most likely because the water bodies are larger than the lower lakes . In contrast to the shallower Erie and Ontario lakes , which flush out their water about every 2 to 7 years , water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to 170 years . <p> The study also confirmed that these chemicals increase in concentration as they travel up the food chain . Algae and plants have the lowest concentration , according to the study , because they grow and die quickly . But predators such as salmon and eagles had the highest concentration because they 're eating a large amount of prey that have a lot of accumulated PFAS . <p> " If we can understand what the PFAS levels are in the food web , we can better communicate the risk of consuming those potentially toxic food sources , " said Katherine Manz , an environmental health professor at the University of Michigan who was not involved in the study . <p> While it was easy to find PFAS data on salmon , trout and some birds , Lamberti said , the information on the " less glamorous " smaller fish , invertebrates and algae was harder to come by . <p> Tools to analyze the range of these chemicals are still evolving , said Vernon Lalone , CEO of Wave Lumina , a Michigan-based startup that 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ soil . <p> " It 's like a chicken-and-an-egg situation , " said Lalone , who was n't involved in the study . " You 've got to have an analytical method that 's robust and reliable enough to measure these things before you can regulate them at certain limits . " <p> Lamberti said there are still plenty of questions about how these chemicals will shift in waterways as temperatures rise due to climate change , ice formation shifts , and as industries introduce new chemicals . But he 's optimistic -- his study shows that when forever chemicals are removed from production , food webs eventually cycle them out . There is no national ban on PFAS , but a patchwork of federal regulations restricts certain chemicals , and some manufacturers have phased out other PFAS compounds voluntarily . <p> " That 's what we need to be thinking about with these chemicals , " Lamberti said , " how we 're going to remove them from the production and find substitutes for them to do the right thing . "

This mirrors the trajectory of Mark Carney from environmental advocate to pipeline proponent , though he had always hedged his climate activism with a view to economic opportunity . <p> In 2019 , as United Nations Special Envoy on Climate Change , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that have long been warning about the risks posed by climate change . Soon after he suspended the federal fossil fuels emissions cap and ended the electric vehicle mandate . <p> Carney has called the green transition " the greatest commercial opportunity of our time . " A world-wide transition to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aim is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by phasing down fossil fuels and switching to low-carbon electricity sources . <p> Carney has put much of that on hold and partnered with Alberta to plan a new pipeline to carry one million barrels of oil a day to an export terminal in British Columbia to serve the burgeoning Pacific region economy and help rescue Canada 's economy in the process . That part of the plan is n't helped by his having changed from a promise that the private sector would build the thing to now saying a private company will have only a 10-per-cent stake in the project . <p> Saying he will work with the oil industry to lessen emissions he , and it , are counting largely on the questionable method of carbon capture and underground storage of oil field emissions . <p> CARNEY 'S see-saw affair with sustainability does come at a time of world economic upheaval that is pulverizing the Canadian economy . But there is no need to so largely betray his earlier position as a climate activist . <p> Many European countries have successfully @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , solar , geothermal and tidal power to largely end dependence on dirty oil . Canada 's current priority is to spend an estimated $40 billion of public money -- and we know how long initial cost estimates last -- to build an oil pipeline that will take years to complete . By that time , much of the world 's dependence on oil will have dried up and only then will come the needed and long overdue large-scale conversion to green energy . <p> NOT to be outdone , Ontario Premier Doug Ford and his Alberta counterpart , Danielle Smith , this week announced their own plans for a pipeline from the oil fields east through the Prairies and Northern and central Ontario to the refineries in Sarnia , roughly double the length of the proposed route from Alberta to the West Coast . <p> Here too there is every likelihood that taxpayers will foot the bill while the oil company users enjoy continued huge profits . That is because there is little likelihood that a private company will be willing to build the so-called Northern Shield Energy Corridor @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not going to make anybody any money , " said Stephen Legault , Environmental Defence Canada 's expert on Alberta 's oil and gas economy . " If it was , then there would be private investors lining up , and there are n't . " <p> Keith Stewart , senior energy strategist for Greenpeace Canada , said the plan makes no sense economically or environmentally . " There is no private-sector proponent for these pipelines because there is no business case in a world where electric vehicles and heat pumps powered by wind and solar energy are cheaper , cleaner and faster to deploy than the fossil fuel megaprojects that are fuelling heat waves and wildfires . " <p> Aside from the future reduction in global oil demand , Sarnia 's refineries would require costly upgrades before they have capacity for the volume of crude oil that this pipeline would deliver . <p> Neither premier could provide a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feasibility study wo n't be completed by the end of 2026 , reports Emmerson Jull in Canada 's National Observer . But Legault believes that spending on the Northern Energy Shield Corridor project could be more than double the Trans Mountain expansion -- which saw $34.1 billion in federal investment -- since the proposed Alberta to Ontario route would be twice its length . <p> THIS LEADS to another question . If we are going to build a pipeline-- and that 's a big if -- why would we build it all the way to Sarnia . The refinery city on the St. Lawrence Seaway at the southern end of Lake Huron features an active deep-water port for both domestic freighters and ocean-going ships . <p> So does Thunder Bay which has just added a new ship facility using the old ore dock in addition to the dynamic Keefer Terminal where a dock rehabilitation project is currently planned and where additional capacity would be logical as it keeps breaking shipping records . <p> Pipeline construction costs through the flat soils of the Prairie provinces would be relatively small compared with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Instead of blasting through the entirety of Northern Ontario , why not take a turn south before having to cross the Nipigon River ( a contentious issue in the failed Energy East pipeline plan ) and build the pipeline to new handling facilities at the Port of Thunder Bay where tankers could take on crude for the trip down to Sarnia ? It would be much cheaper and make better use of the Seaway route that is too often overlooked as a cleaner alternative to trucks and a safer one than rail for moving oil . <p> ALL that said , a pipeline -- any pipeline -- in this day and age is a white elephant in the making . We are in the midst of a climate crisis with huge and unpredictable swings between scorching heat waves with dangerous wildfires and prolonged droughts , and drenching rainstorms causing massive flooding and widespread death . And yet here we are in Canada planning not one but two new oil pipelines that , by the time they come on line , will see a shrunken world market and catastrophic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wonder , ' What were we thinking ? First and foremost , there is significant growing demand and investment opportunities in private infrastructure . So , understanding private infrastructure allows investors and advisors to capitalize on these opportunities . <p> Outside of this great tailwind , there are many other benefits as well . <p> First off , diversification . Private infrastructure assets , such as energy , transportation and utilities , often have low correlation with traditional asset classes like @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ portfolios and help reduce the overall risk for their clients . <p> A second great benefit is also the stable and predictable cash flows , which all of our investors love . Infrastructure investments typically generate steady income through long-term contracts or regulated revenues . This stability is attractive for investors , especially seeking reliable returns and yield over a long term . <p> A third benefit is the inflation protection . Many infrastructure assets have revenues linked to inflation . Examples are tolls , utility rates , the bills that we receive every single month . When you 're investing in these assets , you are ultimately helping your clients protect their portfolios against rising prices , which is an environment that we have been in for a while and expect to be in for years to come . <p> Last but not least , sustainable and responsible investing , which is very important and it 's a growing presence in our portfolios . Infrastructure projects often have direct impacts on the communities that they 're involved in , and the environment . Investors who are seeking assets that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ principles -- if they 're looking for that , private infrastructure offers the best avenue for meaningful impact . <p> * * * <p> Let 's bring it to real-life examples , which I think always helps myself and definitely makes the conversation easier with end clients . <p> Starting off with the inflation protection , private infrastructure provides this protection in really two good ways . <p> One is these many infrastructure assets having their revenues linked to inflation , and this is outlined in their contract . @@138952084 <p> The Sleep Whisperer is a series of columns offering insights and advice about sleep health . It is not a substitute for seeking professional medical care . <p> Heat waves are breaking temperature records in several parts of Canada . As extreme heat events are becoming more common in the context of climate change , you may be wondering how heat affects your health and how to best adapt . What may come as a surprise is that temperature spikes actually have more impacts on our physiology during sleep than when we are awake . Understanding the relationship between heat and sleep may therefore be key to staying healthy in a warming world . <p> Warmer temperature can be bad , but here is why acute heat waves are worse <p> Our body has evolved with some capacity to acclimatize its own temperature in response to progressive changes across seasons , but this process takes time . However , when we face sudden increases in ambient heat , the story is quite different , as our body triggers emergency physiological changes . For instance , blood flow rushes towards @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heat out of the body . To achieve this , our heart needs to rapidly switch gears , working harder and faster . This not only increases cardiovascular risks , but also unbalances the autonomic nervous system in a way that may be less conducive to sleep . Furthermore , sudden temperature peaks can confuse the biological clock , which expects cooling temperatures at night to set the times at which our body is ready to fall asleep and wake up . When high humidity is part of the picture , it makes things even worse as our skin struggles to dissipate our internal body 's heat through evaporating sweat . <p> Sleep 's response to heat <p> All of this has measurable impacts on our sleep . A recent study linking meteorological data to sleep-tracker data in over 300,000 people around the world found that temperatures around 27 Celsius were linked to shorter sleep compared to more temperate weather . In fact , laboratory studies simulating heat waves showed a 14-minute reduction in sleep duration for every 0.1 C increase in core body temperature during the night . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Research consistently shows that acute periods of warmer weather cut the time we spend in deep sleep and REM sleep . This is especially unfortunate since these sleep stages are critical periods when our body regulates its own temperature . If you have sleep apnea , warm nights may also worsen your breathing . <p> Since sleep plays a critical role in many dimensions of health , sleep difficulties triggered by heat waves worsen our susceptibility to other heat-related illnesses . Indeed , research is starting to map associations between how we sleep and the surge of mental health , brain and heart problems during heat waves . <p> Stay hydrated during the day ; this will help your body regulate its temperature more efficiently during the night . <p> Strip down for sleep . The more skin you expose , the more your body will expel heat and humidity . If you do wear pyjamas , opt for cotton fabrics , which are lightweight and breathable . <p> If you do need to nap , keep it short ( e.g. maximum 20 minutes ) and before mid-afternoon . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ you and worsen the effects of heat waves on sleep . <p> Do n't fall into the trap of going to bed earlier after a bad night , as this can further reduce your deep sleep debt related to the heat wave . <p> Embrace the mornings . You may wake up a bit earlier than usual because of the heat . If you feel that you wo n't fall back asleep , get out of bed and start your day rather than lingering in bed . If this creates opportunities to do a bit of light exercise in the morning before the heats gets worse , this may boost your energy levels during the day and protect your sleep . <p> As we can increasingly forecast extreme heat events , there are also things you may be able to set in place before the next heat wave . To mimic natural acclimatization and slowly built heat tolerance , you can build gradual exposure to heat over time in the one to two weeks before heat strikes . This could be done by introducing 1-1.30 hours of exercise in progressively @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have been shown to enhance deep sleep later on when environmental temperatures rise . If you try this , make sure to stay well hydrated during those transitional periods . <p> Of note , both cooling with AC and ventilation with electric fans can improve sleep . You can do your part to slow down global warming by using ventilation when sufficient and leaving AC for the more extreme cases . Also , keep in mind that using AC all summer long may reduce your natural physiological adaptation to heat , which subjects your body to more abrupt temperature shifts when heat waves emerge . <p> Dr. R ? becca Robillard , PhD , is a clinical neuropsychologist and associate professor at the School of Psychology at the University of Ottawa . She also leads clinical sleep research at the Royal mental health hospital . She co-chairs the Canadian Sleep Research Consortium , a national hub of sleep scientists and clinicians.

@@138952485 <h> Tornado alerts on the rise , but could too many warnings lead to alert fatigue ? <p> With Saskatchewan experiencing an active severe weather season and more than 100 tornado warnings already issued this year , some experts are questioning whether an increasing number of alerts could make people less likely to respond when a real threat emerges . <p> According to the Saskatchewan Public Safety Agency ( SPSA ) , 98 emergency alert messages had been issued in Saskatchewan through the national Alert Ready system as of June 30 . Those alerts included 93 tornado warnings , three civil emergency alerts , one flash flood alert and one wildfire alert . The figure does not account for the dozens of tornado and severe weather alerts issued in the last two weeks , as storm activity has continued across much of the province . <p> The warnings are issued by Environment and Climate Change Canada ( ECCC ) and distributed through Alert Ready , Canada 's national public alerting system . Depending on the severity and type of event , alerts can appear on cellphones , television and radio @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ alerts , the warnings that override phone settings and emit a loud tone , are reserved for the most serious weather threats . <p> " Specifically , when there is a tornado warning , that will trigger the broadcast-intrusive alert , " Bilous said . Extremely severe thunderstorms capable of producing destructive winds or very large hail can also trigger the alerts , she added . <p> While the warnings are intended to save lives , some residents have voiced frustration over receiving multiple alerts for the same storm or warnings for weather occurring far from their location . <p> Greg Johnson , a Saskatchewan storm chaser and operator of tornadohunter.com , believes there is a legitimate risk of " alert fatigue " if people receive too many warnings that do n't appear relevant to them . <p> " Absolutely , " Johnson said when asked whether warning fatigue is a concern . <p> " I think that the pendulum has swung so far towards having warnings out of caution that now nobody even pays attention to the things . " <p> Johnson said part of the problem lies in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Unlike the United States , where tornado warnings are often targeted to the projected path of a storm using polygon-based warning areas , Canadian warnings are generally issued for larger forecast regions . <p> That can result in people receiving tornado warnings despite being well outside the area of immediate danger . <p> Johnson recalled receiving a tornado warning while chasing a storm south of Prince Albert even though he was approximately 80 kilometres away under sunny skies . <p> " The warning says , ' Get underground right now to keep yourself safe , ' " he said . " Of course , that does n't make any sense because I 'm looking around and I 'm under blue skies and there 's no tornado anywhere nearby . " <p> He worries repeated experiences like that can lead people to dismiss future warnings . <p> " If you get enough of those , then when something serious does happen , you 're no longer taking it as seriously as you need to . " <p> A tornado alert issued near Onion Lake on July 11 , 2026 included an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ said some communities in the critical alert area may not even see the storm . ( Image Credit : Screenshot/SaskAlert ) <p> Bilous said some of the confusion comes from how the Alert Ready system works through cellular networks . <p> When a tornado warning is issued , phones connected to towers within the affected coverage area receive the alert . As people move between towers , or if multiple towers cover a broader area around the storm , users can receive repeat notifications for the same warning . <p> " That 's why they receive multiple alerts for the same storm , " she said . <p> The SPSA noted that users of the SaskAlert app have options to reduce unwanted notifications . Residents can customize alerts based on specific communities , regions or use the app 's " Follow Me " feature to receive warnings based on their current location while travelling . <p> The agency said the customization tools are intended to help residents receive timely information about emergencies that affect them while reducing alerts for areas that are not relevant . <p> A tornado on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Johnson . ( Image Credit : Submitted/Greg Johnson ) <p> Despite concerns about warning fatigue , Johnson said Canada 's severe weather warning system has improved significantly over the past decade . <p> He noted tornado warnings were once commonly issued only after a tornado had already been reported on the ground . <p> " There has been an incredible improvement , " Johnson said . <p> " It 's not perfect , and certainly there 's maybe this warning fatigue , but it is 1,000 times better than it was even 10 years ago . " <p> For their part , meteorologists and emergency officials continue to encourage residents to take every tornado warning seriously and seek shelter immediately when one is issued , even as discussions continue about how alerting systems can better balance broad public safety with warning precision .

" <p> Health experts are not currently concerned about air quality in Toronto but warn prolonged exposure to moderate risk air may threaten health . <p> The third is through mechanical ventilation systems that funnel outside air indoors , said Jeffrey Siegel , a professor of civil engineering at the University of Toronto . Meanwhile , single family homes and townhouses tend to be " leakier " compared to highrise apartment complexes , Li said . <p> Buildings without air conditioning are also at greater risk if windows are kept open to regulate high temperatures , Siegel added . <h> How to improve indoor air quality <p> The first rule of thumb is to close any doors and windows when it 's smoky out . Reading this Ten-Point Plan did not leave a sense of enlightenment , but a sense of sadness about the direction of the CARICOM region and its development.Independence and development responsibilityJamaica 's independence in 1962 was a time of pride and optimism about the future . As an independent country , Jamaicans were going to build on the infrastructure that was handed over to them and , paddling our own canoe , would build on this moving further towards their development goals . Jamaica had self-government from 1944 . In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ministry of External Affairs , taking over the country 's foreign policy , and defence , taking over the military , the Jamaica Defence Force . Other institutions and industries were in place , including a parliament , courts , police force , prisons , schools/colleges , water , including reservoirs , electricity , public transportation ( bus and railway ) and ports , not perfect , but workable with the expectation of improvements championed by the elected governments.Reflecting on independence led to reviewing two pieces in this column from 2022 when Jamaica marked 60 years of independence from British rule . The view was that the post-independence generations had failed to deliver the anticipated economic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , e.g. the 1970s oil crises . Conventions ' of September 6 , 2023 . It actually also implies that the Africans had no responsibility in slavery either . We are all hapless victims of colonisation and slavery.Reparations , the new development strategyIt now seems that Jamaica 's new development strategy is linked to claims for reparations for colonisation and slavery , which have held back our development since independence . Remedying the public health crisis -- For CARICOM , this is manifested in the high prevalence of non-communicable diseases , inadequate healthcare infrastructure , and the health impacts of climate change . CARICOM asserts that the crisis has its roots in the colonial experience of the mass enslavement of African people , and thus it must be addressed by Britain.5 . Compensation for gender-based violence and assault on family -- CARICOM is demanding from the British government a positive reparatory justice response to the destruction of the right to family lineage and the emotional harm that still affects black communities ; 6 . Psychological rehabilitation -- Britain must repair the psychological trauma caused by the legacies of their crimes against humanity , which have left deep mental and social scars . They must support , through reparations , funding for all initiatives that will promote cultural reclamation and provide a sense of closure and psychological healing to affected populations and communities ; 7 . The right to sovereignty and development : technology , innovation and entrepreneurship - CARICOM demands the right @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on technology , innovation , and entrepreneurship . Debt cancellation , monetary compensation and decolonisation -- CARICOM is demanding monetary compensation , in various forms , from all involved in the trans-Atlantic slave trade , including monarchies , governments , institutions , individuals and others . This must include debt relief . It is noted that most of Jamaica 's external debt , acquired as an independent , sovereign nation , is owed to multilateral institutions and to China . " <p> Chapman says the phenomenon of dry lightning is " highly concerning , " and combined with parched conditions and high winds it could be associated with up to 150 fire starts in a day . As of Wednesday morning , British Columbia had a total of about 20 active fires . <p> Here 's an explanation about dry lightning and why it 's now of such concern . <p> WHAT IS DRY LIGHTNING ? <p> As the name suggests , dry lightning is associated with little or no precipitation . Chapman says that without moisture to inhibit fire growth , firefighters lose the time needed to respond in the early stages of a blaze . <p> Natural Resources Canada says it can result in a destructive cycle -- large fires can produce their own @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ produce dry lightning . <p> WHERE AND WHEN IS IT EXPECTED ? <p> Chapman says that the southeast third of the province can expect high winds and dry lightning " with very little or no precipitation " from Wednesday afternoon into Friday . " <p> While lightning is also expected in the northeast of B.C. , Chapman says fuels there are expected to be " less receptive " to fire starts . <p> HOW ARE FIREFIGHTERS PREPARING ? <p> Chapman says the wildfire service has " all aviation assets engaged , " on alert and ready to respond to new starts . @@139014175 <p> Jeffrey F. Collins is the inaugural director of the Palmer Institute for Canadian Leadership in Charlottetown and author of the 2024 book Canada 's Defence Procurement Woes . <p> Alex Cool-Fergus is a political organizer and climate strategist . <p> As we surveyed the sickly yellow sky in Toronto on Wednesday , coloured by out-of-control wildfires up north , we thought back to the burning season of last year . <p> In August , 2025 , wildfire did to the village of Kingston , N.L. , what two centuries of wars , economic depression and storms could not : wiped much of it off the map . Facilitated by drought ( itself a rarity on an island known for fog and drizzle ) the Kingston wildfire was one of six raging simultaneously across the province that summer . The fires taxed people and equipment alike , especially the decades-old provincial water bomber fleet . <p> Typically equipped with five of the famous Canadian designed and built Canadair CL-215 " super scoopers , " provincial authorities were down a plane due to repairs . In fact , pilot shortages and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bomber fleet between 2018 and 2025 . Yet even if it were available , five water bombers would not have been enough last year . The Kingston fire alone required nine to hold it at bay . It took borrowing and renting additional airpower from across the continent to make up the difference -- hardly a recipe for proactive wildfire planning . <p> It 's a different situation in Ontario today . Premier Doug Ford said 50 firefighting aircraft have been deployed . But the fires grow year after year , and so must our fleets of water bombers . <p> The question , of course , is who will pay for this , and the answer might surprise you : The cost should come out of our defence spending . Here 's why . <p> Where they were previously concentrated in certain swaths of the Canadian boreal forest , severe climate change-induced wildfires are now ubiquitous , invoking a new term in this country 's lexicon : " wildfire season . " <p> This year , Western Canada and the United States are facing extremely low snowpacks and warmer-than-usual @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and federal authorities will have to move quickly . Factor in other wildfire hotspots such as southern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean and the sum impact is a growing demand for water bombers . Hence why the latest version of the workhorse of Canada 's various public and private water bomber fleets for decades , the DHC-515 ( often referred to as a " Canadair " ) , is in high demand . <p> Manufactured by De Havilland Canada near Calgary , and capable of operating in remote regions in a myriad of climates , Canadairs are a popular wildfire fighting asset at home and abroad . In response to France 's 2022 wildfires , President Emmanuel Macron declared , " We need more Canadairs . " De Havilland consequently secured 22 orders from European Union member states . <p> This is obviously good news for a Canadian company , domestic jobs and national pride but less so for those provincial governments seeking to beef up their own aging fleets amid growing financial constraints . It did not have to be this way , however . The lack of local @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the better part of a decade . Now with the Europeans moving first , domestic orders , such as Manitoba 's contract for three Canadairs , wo n't be delivered until the early 2030s . <p> With a now healthy order book , De Havilland will need to boost production capacity to deliver Canadian-made water bombers . <p> Fortunately , Prime Minister Mark Carney 's pledge to boost defence spending to the NATO target of 5 per cent of GDP by 2035 and reinvigorate the defence industrial base provides the financial coverage and policy framework to do just that . Under the NATO target , Canada can dedicate 1.5 per cent of the 5 per cent annual spend to " critical infrastructure ... civil preparedness and resilience . " Water bombers to protect communities from wildfires easily meet this requirement . <p> The government 's recently announced Defence Industrial Strategy likewise identifies aircraft production , maintenance , training and simulation as constituting four of Canada 's 10 " key sovereign capabilities . " With the strategy , the government can prioritize defence spending in those areas where Canada is already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and boost exports . As the world 's first purpose built water bomber , the entire Canadair series represents a globally recognized brand in service throughout the world . <p> The federal spending power and physical footprint through billions in northern military infrastructure spending enables Canada to re-imagine what national defence means in the 21st century where the existential threats to many local communities are not Russian hypersonic missiles but climate-change driven wildfires . The Ontario fires this week must spur us to action . 
@@139014188 <p> Ask a Therapist is a series of columns offering insights and advice about common psychological concerns . It is not a substitute for seeking professional psychological or medical care . <p> As a therapist , I work with many clients struggling with anxiety . More and more , I also hear from people experiencing climate anxiety , a sense of persistent distress about climate change and the future of the environment . It is characterized by fear , grief and a sense of helplessness . Climate anxiety is not a mental health condition , but rather a natural response to a real-world threat . However , if it becomes intense or overwhelming , it can have a major impact on quality of life . According to a study published in October , 2025 , a million Canadians report experiencing climate anxiety severe enough to disrupt their sleep and daily functioning . <p> Signs and symptoms include being constantly fixated on climate news , physical sensations such as a racing heart rate or fatigue , grief about damaging environmental events that result in the loss of habitats , communities and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ individual actions may affect climate change , existential dread or feelings of powerlessness about your ability to have a helpful impact on a global problem . <p> Living with climate anxiety is emotionally heavy , and it is important to practice skills to manage it so that it has less of a negative impact on your functioning . It 's also worth noting that many worries about climate change are realistic , and worry can be helpful if it spurs beneficial action . Coping with climate anxiety involves managing the intensity of anxiety and harnessing it into values-based action . <h> Avoid doomscrolling <p> Being informed is important , yet constantly consuming climate-related news can maintain and intensify anxiety . Reading a couple of key articles is different from doomscrolling or engaging with the same information over and over again . Be aware of how you feel when consuming climate stories , and put limits on your consumption , for example , 15 minutes a day . <h> Talk about how you feel <p> Anxiety can intensify when we do n't have outlets to express it . The weight of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ share how we feel . Identify people in your life who you feel safe and comfortable with and set aside time to talk with them about your difficult emotions . This creates an opportunity for mutual understanding and support . On the other hand , if you are constantly talking about climate anxiety , it may be helpful to shift focus to other topics . <h> Develop additional outlets for releasing anxiety <p> There are many ways to help release anxiety . Here are a few you can try . <p> Intentional breathing decreases nervous system activation and lowers anxiety . You can practice physiological sigh breathing by deeply inhaling through your nose , taking a second short inhale to inflate your lungs fully , and exhaling slowly and completely through your mouth . Repeat for one to three minutes . <p> Journalling can help create space from spiralling thoughts . Set a timer for five to 10 minutes , and write down your thoughts . When the time is up , tell yourself that your thoughts are on the paper and you can leave them there for a bit @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ activity releases mood-boosting chemicals in the brain and can ease muscle tension . You can engage in mindful movement , such as yoga or taking a slow walk outside , or higher intensity movement , such as a brisk walk , jog or bike ride , which can release the physical energy associated with anxiety . <h> Spend time in nature <p> While being in nature and noticing changes to the environment can be distressing , in general , immersing yourself in nature can decrease anxiety , lower stress hormones and provide a relieving break from electronic devices and the news . Get outside . Spend time in a park , amongst trees , or near bodies of water . Research shows that 20 minutes in nature lowers stress . <h> Focus on what you can control <p> Dwelling on what-if or worst-case scenarios raises anxiety and a sense of helplessness . To increase a sense of control , focus on specific and realistic actions you can take , such as becoming involved in local advocacy efforts , using sustainable transportation or reducing household energy waste . Intentional personal choices @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy change that addresses the crisis . <h> Take collective action <p> Social connection supports mental health and well-being . Being around others who share similar values and goals , and taking action together , can increase a sense of self-efficacy and hope . Explore local environmental groups or organizations that you can participate in . It is comforting to know that you are not alone in your anxiety , and many people are dedicated to lessening the impact of climate change . Further , community is essential for building a sense of collective resilience . <h> Balance engagement with rest <p> When the world is on fire , literally and figuratively , it can feel like no amount of work is enough . Yet constantly pushing yourself without taking time to rest and refuel can lead to burnout and an inability to take action . You are not a machine , and there are limits to what you can do in any given moment . By resting , you are allowing yourself to be engaged sustainably . Sit , rest , breathe , drink water , eat regularly , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sleep . <p> Jennifer Caspari , PhD , is a registered psychologist in British Columbia . She works at Tall Tree Integrated Health in Vancouver and is the author of You Are More Than Your Body .

@@139014870 <h> A grief framework can help us cope with climate anxiety . <h> Key points <p> " Eco-grief " related to climate and environmental change is becoming a more common experience . <p> This unprecedented type of grief presents unique challenges and complexities . <p> Psychological understanding must evolve along with environmental and societal changes . <p> As I write this post , smoke obscures what would otherwise be a sunny day here in central New Jersey . An air quality alert marking today 's atmospheric conditions " unhealthy " is in place as smoke from Canadian wildfires blows south and east into many areas of the United States . According to the Canadian Climate Institute , " accelerating climate change , largely from the burning of fossil fuels makes wildfires bigger , hotter , and more destructive " ( Canadian Climate Institute , 2026 ) . Today 's conditions are merely one example of how the planet is changing . As these noticeable changes occur , many of us find ourselves feeling helpless and unnerved as we try to acclimate to an environment that feels increasingly different than it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ attached to not feeling in control and to living in a state of uncertainty , and the data related to climate anxiety support this reality . In the United States , the proportion of individuals worried about climate change increased from 51 percent in 2010 to 64 percent in 2023 ; in the United Kingdom , search queries around " climate anxiety " surged 27-fold in the first 10 months of 2023 compared to the same period in 2017 ( K ? hner et al. , 2025 ) . <h> The Concept of Eco-Grief <p> Climate anxiety is real and prevalent , and if you are a therapist , the topic has likely entered your office , accompanied by a sense of anxiety , hopelessness , and resignation . <p> It might sound strange , but a grieving process can help us cope with this type of worry and despair . Grief , as we now understand it , is not relegated to physical deaths ; rather , it can be experienced during times of transition , and in relation to letting go of the way things used to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of it in terms of fireflies : When I was a child in the 1980s , the summer night sky was often illuminated by fireflies , providing an idyllic summer landscape . These days , I swear I see far fewer fireflies and , many nights , none at all . Recent data from the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation shows that due to a variety of threats including habitat loss , light pollution , pesticide use , and climate change , many firefly species are now at risk of extinction ( Fallon , 2025 ) . When I truly inspect my feelings about this change to the night sky , I can absolutely frame it as a grieving process : What was once there no longer is , and that feels painful , makes me angry , inspires me to take action , and pushes me to find ways to accept a new reality . <p> All of this is almost perfectly in line with " traditional " grieving process we go through when a loved one dies . We might , in a nonlinear fashion , be in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and consider ways to move forward in a different reality . Recently , the phrase " eco-grief " has entered the psychological parlance , and it is , indeed , an apt way to name the grief that can be attached to the complex process of coping with significant and often irreversible changes in our environment . According to Ashlee Cunsolo , director of the Labrador Institute , and Neville Ellis , research fellow at the University of Western Australia , people " experience climate grief when they notice or anticipate the loss of species , ecosystems and meaningful landscapes due to acute or chronic environmental change " ( Cunsolo &amp; Ellis , 2018 ) . Clinical social worker Andrew Bryant adds , " Grief is a normal human reaction to loss or anticipated loss ... The loss of stability or a predictable future -- or anticipating exposure to other people 's loss -- is naturally going to trigger grief " ( Allen , 2021 ) . An acknowledgment and acceptance of " eco-grief " as a real and prevalent manifestation of the grieving process can help us to normalize @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is important to note , however , that this type of grief , having no real precedent , presents some unique challenges and differences from more widely understood types of grief . First , because loss associated with environmental changes is a relatively new concept , it lacks the same types of cultural supports and practices that are in place for more traditional manifestations of grief . So continued exploration of and discussion about this topic is vital to broadening our understanding of climate grief . Second , it is necessary to recognize that certain populations are more susceptible to facing " eco-grief , " particularly indigenous communities and people who make their living off the land . A recent study found that people like climate scientists and members of indigenous communities may be more likely to experience climate grief because they have more intimate knowledge of the ways climate change is already altering the environment ( Chu &amp; Yang , 2019 ) . All this to say that as we acknowledge climate grief as a novel phenomenon , we must continue to learn about its intricacies . <p> As @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can tell you that grief must be witnessed ; if it is left ignored or faced in isolation , it becomes that much harder to cope with in a healthy way . Our understanding of human psychology is constantly evolving and often evolves along with environmental , cultural , or societal changes ( for example , read some of the psychological works of the midcentury and you will see how fears of nuclear annihilation informed psychology at that time ) . Understanding this relatively new type of grief can strengthen our larger understanding of human nature and allow us to support those who are experiencing feelings of grief and loss related to our changing planet .

@@139034803 <h> Weather Alert <p> When indoors , keep windows and doors closed as much as possible . When there is an extreme heat event occurring with poor air quality , prioritize keeping cool . Protect your indoor air from wildfire smoke . Actions can include using the highest quality air filter that your ventilation system can handle and/or a certified portable air cleaner that can filter fine particles . If you must spend time outdoors , limit the time as much as possible . A well-constructed , well-fitting and properly worn respirator type mask ( such as a NIOSH-certified N95 or equivalent respirator ) can reduce your exposure to the fine particles in the smoke . Even though exposure may be reduced , there can still be risks to health . Check in on others who are in your care or live nearby who may be more likely to be impacted by wildfire smoke . @@139045372 <h> GTA enters third day of air quality warning with conditions expected to worsen <h> CTV National News : Here 's how you can protect yourself against smoke inhalation <h> ' Any kind of smoke is bad smoke ' : Climatologist on the health impacts of wildfire smoke <p> The smoke-choked skies blanketing Toronto this week may be a glimpse of what 's to come , as experts say warmer weather and drier forests are making wildfire smoke a more frequent visitor , though the conditions may differ each summer . <h> Climate change to blame for hazy skies : scientist <p> Mike Wotton , a research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service , says Toronto has seen more hazy skies in the last five years due to forest fires than in the previous 20 years . <p> When asked why the city sees smoggier skies every summer , Wotton says it is what was predicted with climate change . <p> " There 's probably multiple facets in terms of answering that , but we are seeing warmer summers overall , and I think you see that on the news @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ records , " he said in an interview . <p> Just this past week Toronto broke a temperature record , where Tuesday saw a high of 35.9 C near Pearson airport , feeling more like 45 with the humidity . The hottest July 14 on record was more than 30 years ago in 1995 , when the temperature rose to 36.8 C. <p> Forest fuels are all burnable materials , from underground roots to treetop branches . <p> The drying effects from a drought can carry over from year to year , he explains , so when there is a lack of moisture , the forest fuels can burn , produce more smoke or create fires that are harder to suppress . Wotton pointed to the fast-spreading forest fires that engulfed parts of the Kawartha Lakes last year as an example , where 27 hectares ( about the size of 50 football fields ) of land burned following damage from a winter ice storm . <p> " That was unusual , " Wotton said . <p> " There was an area of drought there in this part of southern Ontario @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so coming into the spring , it was like , ' Oh , there 's still this pocket of drought here . ' " <h> ' Becoming more normal ' <p> In Greg Evans 's view , summer wildfires are " becoming more normal " and more Canadians across the country are seeing how climate change is increasing the number of wildfires . <p> " We 're also becoming familiar with the increased incidence of extreme temperatures and how this is linked to climate change , " Evans , an engineering professor at the University of Toronto and director of the Southern Ontario Centre for Atmospheric Aerosol Research , said in an interview with CTV News Toronto . <p> " This , to my recollection , is the first time we 've had them occur simultaneously and give us a double whammy or one-two punch , which ( has ) really raised awareness of how prepared we are to deal with these types of incidents in the future . " <p> Tanzina Mohsin , an associate professor of climatology at the University of Toronto , says it can not be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ normal as the severity of wildfire season depends on several variables , pointing to the temperature and the direction the wind blows as a couple of factors . <p> " I can say that Toronto and much of Ontario should prepare for wildfire , smoke , and hazy skies that could be recurring this summer , " she said in an interview . <p> " This does not mean every summer will resemble the same situation , however . Wildfire seasons usually tend to last longer when you have warmer weather and all those other factors or mechanisms . " <p> It 's a question , Mohsin says , she considers every forest fire season : is it going to last longer ? The professor says a warmer spring would cause the snow to melt earlier , drying the vegetation sooner . <p> Looking at what happens in the springtime can help gauge what kind of wildfire season is coming <p> " These are the things that we have to keep monitoring , and these are the things that would give us information about how to take preventive measures for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this summer event , " she said . <h> What are the health impacts ? <p> With the amount of particulate matter seen in Toronto 's air this week , Evans says even with buildings with proper insulation and good filtration systems , the pollution can still seep in . <p> Evans says about a third of that particulate matter could seep into well-ventilated buildings , which is why he recommends keeping all windows and doors closed , and even masking indoors . Mohsin says wearing a mask like an N-95 is best , and advises staying up to date with Environment Canada 's AQHI index . <p> " Other tips are that if you happen to have a central heat and air conditioning system , there 's a filter in there , and if you turn your fan on to run continuously , that 'll make the best use of that filter , " he said . <p> When the concentration of particulate matter is too high , Evans says a person 's defence system gets overwhelmed , and it can lead to inflammation . <p> " When we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ particles . These particles get onto the surface of our lungs . There , our body 's immune system cuts in , and antioxidants try to fight off the oxidative potential of these particles , " Evans aid . <p> Prolonged exposure to high concentrations of air pollution can impact a person 's respiratory and cardiac systems , creating neurodegenerative and cognitive side effects . He adds that the more people are exposed to fine particulate matter , the more vulnerable they become to illness . <p> " That 's not as applicable for a day like ( Thursday ) or the few days we 're having , where it 's very high for a short amount of time , " Evans said . Looking at this week , he says there is a higher risk of seeing acute effects like asthma attacks , strokes , or heart attacks .

" <p> Latimer said she was in the " structured intervention unit " -- also known as solitary confinement -- where incarcerated people are sometimes kept for 20 hours a day , or more . <p> " And then they 're letting them out of their cells onto the range , which is equally hot , " she said . <p> The human-rights complaint was made on the basis that heat has a disproportionate impact on elderly and ill prisoners , she said , or those who take psychiatric medication . <p> The complaint accuses CSC of " impeding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conditioning for inmates in institutions . " The complaint was referred to the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal on July 8 , according to a file shared with The Hill Times . <p> CSC spokesperson Kevin Antonucci told The Hill Times that " CSC takes the actions necessary to prepare for warmer temperatures , " and the department has implemented a number of strategies and best practices designed to address temperatures over the summer months . That includes increasing access to cold water , ice and cool showers ; ' cooldown zones ' that use existing air-conditioned spaces for larger groups of inmates , such as in gyms and program spaces ; mechanical ventilation that circulates cooler air into institutions ; and dehumidifiers . <p> " Additionally , high-temperature environments , such as kitchens and workshops , may be furnished with air conditioning on an as needed basis , " said Antonucci , adding the health of inmates " at higher risk of heat-related complications " are " continuously monitored , " and " CSC regularly assesses the need for additional accommodations . Cloth , medical and surgical masks are also less effective because they do not seal tightly against the face . <p> Ontario 's Emergency Preparedness Minister Jill Dunlop issued a formal request Thursday for assistance to Ottawa " to be prepared to expedite the development of federal resources -- including the Canadian Armed Forces -- to support evacuations if needed . " <h> Air quality prompted cancellations and closures Thrusday night <p> The City of Toronto closed all outdoor and wading pools Thursday , cancelled , postponed or moved outdoor registered programs indoors where possible and kept city daycares and CampTO programming inside .
