Johnston Toronto Star Toronto Star <p> Orange hues dominated the sky and ash rained down on Toronto for the second day in a row , as wildfires continued to spread and rage in northern Ontario . <p> Premier Doug Ford has insisted that his government put its full financial weight behind firefighting efforts , but critics claim the province has lagged in its funding and preparedness for fires that have only gotten worse with climate change . <p> Experts and independent government agency reports point to a much more complicated picture . Larger fires have grown more frequent and damaging than ever before , meaning governments may need to think beyond firefighting on how to manage them . <p> Premier Doug Ford says approximately 190 wildfires are raging across the northern part of the province -- and have already burned through more land than all of last year 's fire season total . ( July 17 , 2026 ) <p> The Canadian Press Toronto Star <p> " Human beings think that we can outsmart Mother Nature , but some of these fires are incredibly intense , like the ones we 're seeing in northern Ontario right now , " said Glenn McGillivray , a professor of disaster and emergency management at York University . <p> As of Thursday afternoon , 177 active fires were burning , fuelled by a stretch of hot , dry weather and high winds . A few wildfires in northwestern Ontario have also forced evacuations , including one that destroyed homes and buildings on Namaygoosisagagun First Nation north of Thunder Bay , where residents fled the flames without government help . <p> Many of the fires were sparked by lightning . Others have been attributed to human activity , which can include unattended bonfires or power lines . <p> In Toronto , air quality has only gotten worse , as smoke from the fires up north billows southward . Soot caked the city Thursday morning , with the Air Quality Health Index peaking at a reading of 30 during the morning rush , more than double yesterday 's peak on a scale of 0 to 10+ . <p> Over the past three days , the provincial government has been working closely with northern Ontario communities , said Nastassia Varela , a spokesperson for Emergency Preparedness Minister Jill Dunlop . <p> " This morning , we have also requested the federal government be ready to deploy the Canadian Armed Forces as we work through a fast-moving and evolving situation ... our government 's top priority is to keep people safe , " Varela said . <h> Is the Ford government doing enough ? <p> Ford defended his government 's firefighting budget , blasting people " on social media " who have accused him of cutting it . <p> " We would never underfund our firefighters ever -- never ever . We 've more than doubled the base funding for emergency firefighting , " Ford said at a groundbreaking for a hospital in Windsor on Thursday , <p> In his eight years in office , Ford has upped funding for emergency firefighting , budget documents show . But , as was practice before Ford entered office , that budget is routinely less than what 's actually needed to actually put wildfires out , and at the end of the year , the actual amount spent is far higher . That 's been the case every year for the past decade , except 2022 . <p> The province spent $271 million battling wildfires last year -- but the province had budgeted just $135 million . For this year , the province has budgeted $150 million for emergency firefighting . <p> Fire rangers have previously criticized this method of emergency planning , and told the Star last year that it can often lead to last-minute scrambles for helicopters and planes that could have been leased in advance . <p> The FireRanger program is understaffed and over budget , increasing the risk that each new blaze <p> On Thursday , Ford noted his government had earmarked $650 million for five new helicopters and six water bombers . <p> A spokesperson for Natural Resources Minister Mike Harris said the province has added " nearly 170 permanent fire personnel since 2024 " and has an existing fleet of " over 50 aircraft , including helicopters and waterbombers . " <h> Wildfires grow larger , more devastating <p> Over the past decade , wildfires in Canada have gotten worse . <p> Data from the Canadian National Fire Database shows there are fewer total fires in Canada , but wildfires are now burning larger than before . According to the Ministry of Natural Resources , Ontario saw 643 wildland fires in 2025 , lower than the 10-year average , but saw 597,654 hectares of land burned , an area larger than Prince Edward Island . <p> The growing problem is mostly , but not entirely , fuelled by climate change , said Mike Flannigan , a B.C. research chair at Thompson Rivers University who specializes in fire science . <p> Fire is natural in the forests that cover most of Ontario , but decades of fire suppression have left many cluttered with fuel that 's ready to ignite . Climate change , meanwhile , brings longer , hotter fire seasons . Those warmer temperatures fuel more lightning , which can ignite new fires and suck the moisture out of forests so they burn easily and quickly . <p> " This is a new reality , " Flannigan said . " There is going to be more fire and smoke in the future . " <p> Computer models have failed to predict a series of " impossible " blazes -- which means more places <p> Ontario 's Ministry of Natural Resources prioritizes fires based on how likely they are to harm people or critical infrastructure , which Flannigan said is " one of the best ways to approach it . " Sometimes , if a fire poses a low risk , it 's best to let it burn , he added . <p> " I think the public has this expectation that we can put out all the fires all the time , " he said . " I do n't think that 's true , and nor should we . To be honest , we should be letting some of those fires play their natural role . " <h> Too little , too late <p> For fires that do pose a risk to communities , extra funding can help efforts to extinguish them . But those resources need to be in place early to tackle new fires while they 're still small , Flannigan said . <p> " Even when things are extreme , you have a window , " he said . " Sometimes it 's a short window , like 30 minutes . If you get resources to the fire within that 30 minutes , you generally can put it out . " <p> At a certain point , however , uncontrolled fires can become too big for crews to control , no matter how much funding is available , said McGillivray , also the managing director of the Institute for Catastrophic Loss Reduction . <p> The 2024 Jasper fire , for example , was so hot it created its own weather system , with turbulence that made it even more difficult for air tanker crews to battle the flames . <p> " The turbulence was so bad that their heads were hitting the sides of the cockpit , " McGillivray said . " Then when they dropped their load , it was blowing horizontally back into the fire and evaporating . " <p> Instead , governments could better protect communities by making them less flammable , McGillivray said . Simple measures like creating firebreaks and using fire-resistant building materials can make a huge difference . <p> " This is not a huge mystery , " he said . " We know exactly what to do . We just really do n't do it . " <p> Flannigan said in general , governments need to be more proactive . Experts can predict the weather conditions that lead to new fires , he said , meaning governments could create an early warning system and move resources to high-risk areas before anything ignites . <p> " We should ask the question as Canadians : Is the status quo the best option ? " Flannigan asked . <p> A FEDEX employee wearing a mask packs up his trolley as he arrives at his truck on Spadina , Thursday , July 16 , 2026 <p> Sophie Bouquillon/Toronto Star Toronto Star <p> When Adam Kadir left home Thursday morning to work as a carpenter at a west-end construction site , he immediately noticed the air was smokier and heavier than the day before . <p> At 7 a.m. , his supervisor sent a message in the construction company 's group chat acknowledging the poor air quality and telling employees they could decide whether to come to work . <p> Kadir , 25 , decided to show up . He said he was young and had worked the previous day without any issues . But after about an hour outside without a mask and three hours indoors , he became dizzy and felt intense pressure in his head , ending his shift early . <p> " In the beginning , you can still breathe , but the air definitely smells smoky , " said Kadir . " But the longer you are outside , it gets worse and worse . " <p> But even as the city closed outdoor pools , pulled lifeguards from beaches , and cancelled or rescheduled outdoor programs , thousands of people like Kadir -- including construction workers , delivery couriers , landscapers and garbage and recycling collectors -- could still be seen working outside across the city , many without masks or with only a scarf covering their mouth and nose . <p> Experts say this puts them at a unique risk , and they need to be protected . <p> A worker at the RBC Amphitheatre told the Star they are frustrated that the venue is still going ahead with tonight 's Tim McGraw concert , saying they are concerned about working in the current environment . <p> The Star is not naming the worker because they fear speaking publicly could jeopardize their job . A spokesperson for Live Nation , which runs the venue , said in an email that the safety of their employees is a top priority . <p> " We have advised staff that if they do not feel comfortable coming to work due to air quality conditions , they are not required to do so , " the spokesperson added . <p> " It has been communicated that requests for additional breaks , early departures , or other reasonable adjustments will be accommodated as needed . N95 masks are also readily available for all staff . " <p> " I need money more than anything else , " the worker said , explaining why they decided to work on Thursday . The worker added their supervisor gave employees the option not to work and will provide N95 masks on-site . <p> Deena Ladd , executive director of the Toronto Workers ' Action Centre , said the poor air quality is resulting in a situation where some people can stay home but others do n't have a choice , similar to what occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic . <p> " To me this whole situation speaks to the role of the government in stepping in and protecting people who do n't have a lot of voice and protection at work , " she said . <p> Workers have the right to refuse unsafe work , and if they are in a union , a health and safety rep can help with this , she said . But without one , workers may be afraid to say they are n't comfortable with performing what they consider to be risky tasks . <p> Under the Occupational Health and Safety Act , employers have to take every precaution reasonable to protect workers from outdoor hazards : including ensuring people have access to personal protective equipment such as N95 masks , and are able to take breaks , Ladd said . <p> Ideally , the Ministry of Labour would step up with public messaging to employers that they need to take this threat seriously , she added . <p> Otherwise , it 's " putting individuals in a really difficult situation , " Ladd said . " It 's hard for people to be able to speak out without jeopardizing their jobs . " <p> Since 2019 they have increased maximum workplace safety fines , they added . <p> " During periods of elevated heat or poor air quality , employers should ensure workers have access to water , shaded or cool rest areas , training to recognize the signs and symptoms of heat stress and the appropriate level of personal protective equipment . Workers also have the right to refuse unsafe work . " <p> A spokesperson for delivery app DoorDash said in an email that because delivery people choose their own schedules and what deliveries to accept , " no individual is obligated to work when subpar air quality exists . " <p> " We encourage Dashers to consult air quality guidance from the government of Canada to make an informed decision about whether or not to dash , " they added . <p> Dr. Farhan M. Asrar , a family physician and public health physician , and the associate dean at the Toronto Metropolitan University School of Medicine , said outdoor workers " are at greater risk of being exposed to smoke-related , harmful particles . " <p> This can cause a range of symptoms including coughing , shortness of breath , chest pain , headaches and dizziness as well as worsen existing health issues like asthma , heart disease and diabetes . <p> Employers can protect workers by staying informed about air-quality warnings , providing N95 masks and even rescheduling outdoor work for another time , if possible , he added . <h> Which mask protects best against wildfire smoke ? How to stay safe as Toronto 's air is compared to smoking cigarettes <p> Smoke from wildfires -- which are burning more of Northern Hemisphere as Earth warms -- attacks nearly every system in the human body , killing tens of thousands of people a year . ( July 17 , 2026 ) <p> AP Video Toronto Star <p> While the skies over Toronto are looking clearer , Environment Canada still has an air quality warning in place . <p> On 9 a.m . Friday , exposure to the air for a 24-hour period carried roughly the same mortality risk as smoking 4.1 cigarettes , according to website How Many Smokes ? The calculation , which is updated constantly , is based on research by Berkeley Earth , which suggests breathing in 22 micrograms per cubic metre of fine particulate matter for 24 hours carries approximately the same mortality risk as smoking one cigarette . <p> In the short term , exposure to the smoke may cause eye and throat irritation , headaches , difficulty breathing , coughing and chest pain . Over time and after repeated exposures , the smoke could increase our risk of heart and cardiovascular disease , certain cancers , overall reduced lung function and potentially even developmental issues for children . <p> As smoke from wildfires in northwestern Ontario continue to drift across the province , experts urged people to stay indoors and avoid physical exertion outside if possible . <p> " At these very high levels , even well-ventilated , well-filtered buildings can have poor air quality , " said Greg Evans , director of the Southern Ontario Centre for Atmospheric Aerosol Research and a professor at the University of Toronto , on Thursday . <p> Many Torontonians are wondering how to stay safe amid the smoke , so we asked the experts . Here 's what they said . <h> Limit your time spent outdoors <p> As forests burn , they release great plumes of gases , water vapour and fine particulates into the air , which can travel thousands of kilometres from the site of the flames . <p> This smoke can contain dangerous chemicals including carbon monoxide , ammonia and ozone . But the vast majority of wildfire smoke , about 90 per cent of it , is composed of fine particulate matter smaller than the width of a human hair . <p> These particulates , known as PM2.5 ( as they are less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter ) , are the main health risk of wildfire smoke . They 're so small that they can penetrate deep into lungs and even enter our bloodstream ; from there , they can harm our heart , lungs and other organs , increasing our risk of heart attack , stroke and other illnesses . <h> Who is most vulnerable to wildfire smoke ? <p> People with an existing illness or chronic health conditions , such as lung or heart conditions <p> People aged 65 and older <p> Infants and young children <p> Pregnant people <p> People with increased likelihood of exposure due to location or occupation , like people living in rural and remote areas or those who work outdoors . <p> People living in situations of lower socioeconomic status , like those experiencing housing insecurity , those with lower income and those with lower education . <p> The best way to protect yourself is to limit exposure time to the smoke , said Madeleine Orr , an assistant professor of kinesiology and sport ecology at U of T. <p> " The big thing is to limit how much air pollutant content you 're actually taking into your lungs , " she said . Orr recommended spending no more than two hours total outdoors per day , acknowledging this may not be possible for people who work outside . <p> She also advises avoiding heavy physical exercise outside . " Anything that would have you huffing and puffing would be something to avoid . <h> Some masks can help protect you from wildfire smoke , but not all <p> A well-fitted , high-quality mask , such as an N95 mask or respirator , can help in filtering out harmful PM2.5 , said Jeffrey Siegel , a U of T professor who researches indoor air quality . However , not all masks are made the same . <p> " The fit is really important . Unfortunately , the blue surgical masks do n't really offer much of a benefit because the particles at issue are small enough to go through them , and especially around the gaps where they fit the face , " Siegel said . <p> Whether you need a mask or not depends on how much exposure you 'll have to smoke , Orr said . If you 're generally healthy and are going out for a 20-minute walk with your dog , " I 'm not too concerned , " she said . But if you work outdoors all day , if you 're vulnerable to smoke or if you 're exerting yourself outside , " you probably should wear a mask . " <p> People especially vulnerable to smoke , like the elderly or those living with respiratory conditions like asthma or COPD , can consider masking up even when indoors , Evans said . <h> Close windows and doors -- unless it 's extremely hot inside <p> There 's a bit of nuance to this recommendation . Usually , it 's a good idea to close your doors and windows to limit the amount of smoke getting inside . But this week 's smoke coincides with a heat wave in Toronto , and extreme heat indoors can be worse for you than smoke exposure , Siegel said . <p> If you do n't have air conditioning and feel you 'll overheat without cracking open a window , it might be worth the tradeoff in air quality . " It 's a real judgment call , " Siegel said . " Extreme heat is worse , but particles are really bad too . You 've got to strike a balance . " <h> Keep your fan running <p> If you are fortunate enough to have a central air cooling and heating system in your home , Evans recommends having the fans run continuously . " You 'll be making the best use of the filter that 's already in your own system , and those fans push through a lot of air . " <p> " The portable filters are fantastic , " Evans said . " They 're in fact , in some ways , better than central filters because you can locally clean a space quite well . You can pick your bedroom or your living room or whatever is your sanctuary and run portable filters there . " <p> If you 're looking to buy a filter , look for a device certified by the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers ( AHAM ) , according to Health Canada . <h> Set your car 's ventilation to " recirculate " <p> If you 're driving while the air quality is bad , Evans advises setting the ventilation system to recirculate air " so you 're not bringing in outside air . " <h> To shower after going outside or not ? <p> A dermatologist previously told the Star that the harmful particles and chemicals within smoke can irritate and damage the skin , especially those with sensitive skin , allergies or conditions such as eczema or rosacea . <p> Some social media posts recommend showering after being outside in the smoky air , to remove particles from the skin . Evans said the main concern with smoke is inhalation , not its impact on our skin , so showering is n't necessary . But Orr said if you 're spending a good deal of time outside , " that 's not a bad idea . <p> " It takes quite a lot of exposure time to accumulate anything that would really be deleterious , unless you 're in a situation where you 're experiencing a prolonged period of smoke and it 's on your skin all the time , " Orr said . " If it 's one day of bad weather , it 's probably not enough to hurt you . " <p> On Wednesday , Anishinabek Nation Grand Council Chief Linda Debassige said that many community members were forced to flee without the support of emergency services . Chief Lawrence Wanakamik , leader of Whitesand First Nation said his community members took matters into their own hands and started evacuating on Monday before the Ministry of Natural Resources ( MNR ) gave the order . <p> Minnesota Governor Tim Walz thanked Ontario Premier Doug Ford in a post on Wednesday for helping to evacuate two groups of American YMCA campers who were stranded near the U.S.-Canadian border due to the wildfires . <p> Premier Ford is set to speak about Ontario 's wildfire response at 11 a.m . <p> With files from Amarachi Amadike and The Canadian Press <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Updated 2 hrs ago <h> Toronto 's global air quality ranking <p> By Star Staff <p> Here 's where Toronto ranks for worst air quality globally , according to the Air Quality Index . <p> GlobalMedic is sending firefighting equipment to help battle the raging wildfires in northern Ontario . <p> 32 fire skids started arriving into the province on Monday , the Canadian charity posted online . @@139094951 <h> Weather Alert <p> When indoors , keep windows and doors closed as much as possible . When there is an extreme heat event occurring with poor air quality , prioritize keeping cool . Protect your indoor air from wildfire smoke . Actions can include using the highest quality air filter that your ventilation system can handle and/or a certified portable air cleaner that can filter fine particles . If you must spend time outdoors , a well-constructed , well-fitting and properly worn respirator type mask ( such as a NIOSH-certified N95 or equivalent respirator ) can reduce your exposure to the fine particles in the smoke . Even though exposure may be reduced , there can still be risks to health . Check in on others who are in your care or live nearby who may be more likely to be impacted by wildfire smoke . Always follow guidance from local authorities . Learn more at https : **30;687;TOOLONG . Localized poor air quality and reduced visibility due to wildfires may return by this evening and continue through tonight . A major improvement is expected on Sunday . Air @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over short distances and from hour to hour . ### As smoke levels increase , health risks increase . Limit time outdoors . Consider reducing or rescheduling outdoor sports , activities and events . You may experience mild and common symptoms such as eye , nose and throat irritation , headaches or a mild cough . More serious but less common symptoms include wheezing , chest pains or severe cough . If you think you are having a medical emergency , seek immediate medical assistance . People more likely to be impacted by wildfire smoke , including people aged 65 and older , pregnant people , infants and young children , people with an existing illness or chronic health condition , and people who work outdoors , should reduce or reschedule strenuous activities outdoors and seek medical attention if experiencing symptoms . @@139114189 <h> Opinion ' Turn toward Jasper and suddenly you 're in the middle of the apocalypse ' <h> Opinion <p> Two years ago , a wildfire raced through Jasper so fast it did n't burn the trees all the way to the ground . They are still standing , a haunting reminder that Canada 's wildfire crisis is n't going anywhere . <p> Jaime Watt is the Chairman and Founder of Navigator Ltd. and a political strategist . He is a freelance contributing columnist for the Star . <p> No matter how many photographs you 've seen of Jasper , Alberta , after the wildfire , nothing prepares you for the extent of the devastation . It simply silences you . Sadly , I speak from recent experience . <p> Picture this . You 're driving up what many say is the most beautiful road in the world , Alberta 's Highway 93 . There are bears , mountain goats not to be confused with mountain sheep and elk feeding on lush vegetation . <p> Then you turn toward Jasper and , suddenly , you 're in the middle of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the eye can see because after the wildfire broke out two years ago on July 22 , 2024 , it raced through so fast it did n't burn the trees all the way to the ground . They are still standing , a haunting reminder that Canada 's wildfire crisis is n't going anywhere . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Wildfires encroaching into the townsite of Jasper in 2024 forced an evacuation of the national park and destroyed more than 300 of the town 's approximately 1,100 structures . <p> Amber Bracken/The Canadian Press file photo Toronto Star <p> Canadians know this and it frightens them . The Fort McMurray fire was 10 years ago . Slave Lake burned 15 years ago . Yet the federal government has responded with half-measures , moving much slower than the pace of climate change itself . Our country has been hit with back-to-back-to-back record-breaking wildfire seasons in 2023 , 2024 , and 2025 . And , as I write this column , looking out my window in downtown Toronto the sky has been turned a frighting surreal colour that ought to exist in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ burning in Northwestern Ontario . <p> So far , Prime Minister Mark Carney has shown himself willing to fund a visible , deployable wildfire response . This summer , Canada leased 10 new aerial firefighting aircraft . Having them on-call is a meaningful step to support the country 's surge capacity . <p> The Maligne Lodge in Jasper Alberta owned and operated by the Decore family since 1961 burns in 2024 . <p> Karyndecore/Instagram Toronto Star <p> But as I wrote in this newspaper two summers ago , there are not enough water bombers in the world to extinguish all the fires that start burning in what has come to be called " wild fire season . " <p> So what 's the answer to Canada 's wildfire crisis : Stop the fires before they start . And this requires a different approach altogether : structural change . One that 's never been government 's forte . But it just might be Prime Minister Carney 's . <p> This is the prime minister who removed federal barriers to internal trade and created a fast-track mechanism to approve " nation-building " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't a plan and nostalgia is not a strategy . " <p> What Carney must do is take heed of the 15 recommendations in the recent Senate report " Canada on Fire . " They are thoughtful , thorough , and timely -- the Upper Chamber at its finest . The central recommendation is that Canada must create a federal co-ordinating office for wildfires and emergency response , modelled after those in the United States and the United Kingdom , among others . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Some Canadians might bristle at the creation of another new government body . However , the status quo means Canada 's provinces , territories , municipalities , Indigenous communities and governments are not working in sync . <p> The Senators heard from people who know that this lack of co-ordination is directly tied to delayed response times , inconsistent planning , uneven access to equipment and personnel , and a system that mobilizes only once disaster is already underway . <p> What Ottawa should take away from the report is that inaction has had consequences ; but it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ establish a national wildfire hazard mapping program like it has to predict droughts and floods . It should also create a national reforestation strategy . <p> Critically , it must consult Indigenous communities , who have deep knowledge and expertise in fire management . Indigenous firefighting forces should be supported and expanded . <p> Typically , after a crisis like the Jasper wildfire , people expect accountability . They have questions and demand answers . Did you determine what happened and do something about it ? Did you hold someone accountable ? Did you make everyone whole ? Did you review your policies to make sure they were sufficiently robust ? @@139149516 <p> During the inaugural Camp Wavelength music festival on Toronto Island in 2015 , I wandered from my tent around midnight seeking peace near the Gibraltar Point lighthouse . Alone , separated from the din of the city by Lake Ontario and with buoyant echoes of Do Make Say Think 's set still floating around in my ears , I spotted movement in the distance . A cautiously loping coyote stepped out from the bushes under a lamp on the path . We gazed at each other briefly , and it slunk back into the darkness . <p> The memory is hazy , enough for me to wonder if it ever happened at all . I was convinced coyotes could absolutely not find their way to Toronto Island . But Dan Werb 's new book , Our Wild Familiars , has assured me that when it comes to synanthropes , nearly anything is possible . Werb notes that the word " synanthrope " is derived from the Greek for " together with man , " and refers to a wild creature that has " found a way to survive and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The Vancouver-born , Toronto-based epidemiologist , policy analyst , and musician came across the word while writing The Invisible Siege ( 2022 ) , about the proliferation of coronaviruses . Naturally , that book deals with unsettling developments . But in his research for The Invisible Siege , he recognized the massive influence that the movement of animals , forced or natural , has on humankind . After the insular experiences of pandemic lockdown and writing about the causes of those lockdowns , he was seeking a project that would force him out into the world . Synanthropes became the point of departure . <p> " I wanted to make sure that this book was about connection rather than stoking fear or anxiety , " Werb says . " It 's really about how we can feel more intimate and connected with the places we live . " <p> Our Wild Familiars offers an enchanting deep dive into the ways synanthropes shape and are shaped by cities . Certainly , there 's some gloom , which descends mainly through examples of the way that climate change is sowing chaos by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ swiftly . But the cumulative effect of Werb 's globe-trotting efforts to get in front of a kaleidoscopic array of synanthropes is acute wonder , brought on by tales about Toronto 's genius raccoons , the breakneck evolution of New York City rats , juvenile hamadryas baboons riding dogs in Saudi Arabian trash heaps , and why , in the Sundarbans mangrove forest , encroached upon by megacity Kolkata 's creeping sprawl , tigers may have developed a taste for human flesh . <p> The book is anti-doom without sacrificing realistic perspectives . Of its many examples , Werb says his time searching for a giant Pacific octopus under the waves of Seattle 's Elliott Bay was particularly resonant . <p> " It 's a true apocalypse under the ocean , " Werb says . " It 's so polluted , there 's so much garbage , and it just seems like a world of complete devastation . And the fact that it 's not , that one of the most beautiful , intelligent creatures on earth has decided that that is where it wants to live , is incredibly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ melts my heart . " <p> Werb deftly weaves these instances together with the requisite science to express the great connectedness of things , but that fact naturally unravels throughout . Refreshingly , he trades in practical advice and possible solutions . Cities need more " stepping-stones , " island-type habitats that can help animals move safely through them , as urban areas should be understood as fragile , diverse ecosystems that are often more biodiverse than the areas that surround them and central to conservation efforts . There will also be no one-size-fits-all solution for every city -- he says hard-line expressions of conservation biology fail in the face of the tragedy of the Sundarbans " tiger widows , " for example . Wholly shifting to the other side of the spectrum and determining the value of projects based entirely on human benefit wo n't work either . <p> As Our Wild Familiars proves , considering synanthropes in our city planning as the world changes is only going to become more vital . It also sounds fun . There are ways to rejuvenate human relationships with synanthropes infrastructurally in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's Kinder Land Bridge and Prairie , which helps coyotes , armadillos , and opossums cross the city 's Memorial Drive and provides hiking trails for the bipedal among us . Werb 's research has given him the hopeful energy to advocate for projects like this while opposing damaging ones -- for example , he says the effort to expand the Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport is " slimy " and that it will have massive environmental impacts if it goes ahead . <p> " Where I hope this book lives is in getting people feeling like the neighbourhoods they live in , the cities and towns they live in really do matter , " Werb says . " They are important and beautiful places that should be conserved , and the animals and plants that live in them should be the subject of conservation efforts . " <p> The primary gift of the book is to shatter the myth that the city is separate from the natural world , and that we city-dwellers are so different from its synanthropic citizens . In the coyote section , Werb describes his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Los Angeles ' Griffith Park , and the bubbling up of a particular primal feeling it inspired . As his California coyote disappears into the wilderness silently the way my own Toronto Island one did , he recognizes a kinship -- abstract , maybe , but one that acknowledges a shared plight -- and finds a way to name the minor lament welling up in him : " the feeling of not having howled. "

@@139150112 <p> This month , as the United States celebrated its 250th anniversary , the immortal phrase " we the people " appeared on parade banners , in commemorative essays , in speeches , and across celebrations . The phrase evokes the possibility that people across a diverse society can hold a meaningful identity in common . Even beyond the United States , in countries around the world , " we the people " is shorthand for the idea of the shared public good . <p> Still , at a time of deep polarization and political gridlock , those three words that form the opening of the preamble of the Constitution can feel more and more elusive as an everyday reality . <p> Looking at the state of societies globally , it 's now an open question : <p> Is " we the people " still possible ? <p> Or are we more realistically consigned to a world of " us versus them " ? <p> It 's easy to conclude that " us versus them " is one of the oldest features of human nature . We are group-forming beings @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This is part of how people have survived , organized , and defended themselves across history . The fact is that it 's easier to organize people when there 's an " other . " <p> Consider the challenge of climate mobilization . For a time , many climate campaigners tried to frame the climate crisis as requiring a " World War II -- style mobilization . " The point was understandable -- climate change is an existential threat that demands shared sacrifice , public investment , technological transformation , and a willingness to act beyond short-term self-interest . <p> Yet the analogy exposed something about group psychology . World War II mobilization was sustained by a literal human enemy . There was an opposing force people could name , see , fear , and fight . Climate change does n't present itself in the same way . It 's a systematic challenge where there 's no single villain whose defeat would solve the problem . <p> The psychology of " us versus them " can generate intensity , sacrifice , and solidarity in ways that appeals to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ confirms this . In Henri Tajfel 's " minimal group " experiments , people showed favouritism toward members of their own group even when the groups were assigned on trivial or arbitrary grounds . People do n't need much reason to form an " us . " And once there is an " us , " a " them " can quickly emerge , because group identity often gains strength through contrast . <p> The same longing for belonging that brings people into community can also be redirected into exclusion , fanaticism , and violence . When people feel unseen , humiliated , displaced , or powerless , a demagogue can offer a counterfeit form of belonging by giving them someone to blame . <p> I have come to think of this as the shadow side of belonging . <p> It looks like connection , and it may even feel like connection at first . It can offer a shared language , a shared enemy , and a shared sense of purpose . Yet this kind of belonging is hollow because it builds cohesion for some by denying dignity or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ being part of something larger , but only by narrowing the circle of moral concern . <p> Yet this is n't the whole story of human nature . <p> Many of the problems that most require collective action -- including climate , but also AI , inequality , loneliness , and democratic distrust -- do n't come with a simple enemy . They require a broader and more mature form of belonging . They require something bigger than unity against an adversary . They require commitment to a shared future . <p> And , thankfully , human beings also raise children together , mourn together , build institutions for public service , and make sacrifices for people we will never meet . Beyond tribalism , we are also wired for care , collaboration , mutual aid , and compassion . <p> The key psychological question is which identity becomes most salient . Are we primarily insiders and outsiders , winners and losers ? Or can we also remember that we are neighbours , citizens , parents , workers , caregivers , and members of one human family ? <p> Here @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ never fixed . They can narrow , but they can also widen . Under the right conditions , people can come to see former strangers as part of a larger " we . " <p> So how do we promote an ethos of " we the people " that 's grounded in genuine belonging ? <p> First , we need to get beyond online sorting systems that profit from sorting people into opposing camps . Personalized feeds can expose us to different villains , different facts , and different moral realities . We need to create more shared attention in everyday life , through meeting places and shared practices like libraries , community meals , service projects , neighbourhood walks , sports leagues , rituals , and public spaces where people encounter one another as real human beings . <p> Second , we need to solve real problems together . People build trust when they work side by side cleaning up a park , rebuilding after a flood , mentoring young people , caring for elders , serving meals , planting trees , or deliberating over a local budget . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the wider " we . " This is the perennial moral calling to put ourselves in another person 's shoes . It can begin with intellectual humility , like admitting , " I might be wrong . " It can mean asking , " What fear , wound , loyalty , or need might be underneath the troubling behaviour that I see ? " It 's the ethic of seeking to understand . Understanding is not the same as condoning . It is the beginning of responding to the conditions that allow destructive forms of belonging to take hold . <p> Overall , we need to build belonging into the institutions that shape our lives . Schools , workplaces , media platforms , faith communities , governments , and businesses all help determine whether people feel respected , rooted , heard , and able to exercise agency . Belonging can not depend solely on individual goodwill ; it must also be supported by the systems through which we live together . <p> " We the people " has never been complete -- in virtually any society I know of . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has been incomplete does n't mean it 's impossible . It means it 's a practice , a discipline , and a moral and psychological vision that we have to work to make real .

@@139167812 <h> High pressure system trapping wildfire smoke over Prince George , relief possible later this week <p> PRINCE GEORGE -- Prince George residents are being urged to take precautions as wildfire smoke continues to impact air quality across the region , with meteorologists pointing to a persistent high-pressure system as the main reason smoke is lingering over central British Columbia . <p> Matt Loney , a meteorologist with Environment and Climate Change Canada , says a ridge of high pressure has become established over the province , creating the conditions needed for smoke to accumulate near ground level . <p> According to Loney , the weather pattern is bringing both hot temperatures and stable atmospheric conditions . Air beneath the ridge slowly sinks toward the surface , compressing the atmosphere and trapping pollutants in a concentrated layer close to the ground . <p> " That tends to effectively trap pollutants where they are , " said Loney . <p> The situation is being made worse by relatively light winds , which are expected to continue for the next couple of days . Without stronger winds to disperse the smoke , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reducing air quality and visibility across many regions , including Prince George . <p> Loney says smoke conditions can vary significantly , even within the same community . In much of B.C. , geography plays a major role in determining where smoke travels and how concentrated it becomes . <p> Valleys , which are common throughout the province , can act as funnels that direct smoke either toward or away from communities depending on wind direction . Even small shifts in local winds can bring noticeable changes in air quality . <p> " If the wind shifts for any length of time , you might get an improvement in air quality , " Loney explained . " If it comes from the source of the fire , then you would get a degradation . " <p> Time of day also affects smoke concentrations . During daylight hours , the atmosphere becomes less stable , allowing smoke to disperse somewhat . At night , however , cooler temperatures create a stable layer near the surface that compresses smoke closer to the ground . <p> " We feel it in the mornings @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recommend limiting outdoor activity when air quality reaches moderate or worse levels . Loney says extra caution should be taken by seniors , young children and people with compromised immune systems or underlying health conditions . <p> However , he notes that smoke can also affect otherwise healthy individuals . <p> " That particulate in the air is not good at all for lung tissue , " he said . <p> Residents are encouraged to keep windows closed when possible and spend time in air-conditioned buildings with filtered air , such as community centres , malls or libraries . <p> While smoke may remain a concern as long as wildfires continue to burn , there is hope for improvement later this week . <p> Loney says a cold front is expected to move across British Columbia from northwest to southeast , bringing cleaner air from the Pacific Ocean behind it . <p> " We do expect to see an improvement in air quality , even as early as tomorrow , but likely Thursday and beyond , " he said .

The biggest wildfires in the province 's history , labeled Thunder Bay 36 , 54 and 56 and Dryden 34 and 35 , have forced First Nations from their homes and sent billowing smoke to blanket the northeast all the way to Washington and make Toronto smell like a campfire . <p> In his 2023 book Fire Weather , author John Vaillant argued that Canada 's oil industry was tempting fate by developing both the oil sands and a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ naturally flammable ecosystem that is dependent on fire to renew itself . ( The cones of both jack pine and lodgepole pine trees need fire to open and release their seeds . ) The forest was always going to burn . <p> Now Canada 's forest industry , a pillar of our economy since colonial times , must also look itself in the mirror . First Nations have long harnessed fire to manage the forests ; the Secw ? pemc peoples of British Columbia 's interior , for example , used fire to limit forest encroachment on grasslands , stop sagebrush spread and improve forage for hooved game . Settlers banned this practice , however , and for more than a century since , we have sought to suppress fires -- yes , to safeguard communities , but also to protect the forests from ignition , so as to maximize forest products for our pulp , paper and lumber mills . This has increased the flammability of our forests , and the danger that they will burn out of control . <p> In the boreal forest , mechanized logging machines @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ industry argues that these techniques emulate natural disturbance , i.e. the fires and storms that periodically wipe out forests . After they are logged , legions of youth -- brave industrial athletes whose ranks include my son -- fan out each summer to replant trees . This all works , to a point . But the forests we grow back are homogenous and the same age , and thus more flammable . <p> Across Canada ( except in Quebec ) , the forest industry also uses aircraft to spray the newly planted Crown forests with glyphosate , better known by its commercial name , Roundup , to suppress leaf trees , such as poplar and birch , which grow naturally after disturbance . The industry wants only conifers to grow , for the mills ; leaf trees are competition . But leaf trees are also less flammable ; witness the comparative rarity of forest fires in our leaf-dominant forests in the south of eastern Canada . When we kill leaf trees in the boreal forest , we increase fire risk . <p> So does that mean the Americans are right @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a U.S. Congressman from Michigan , fumed at the smoke blanketing his border state , and blamed Canada for abdicating its " responsibility to prevent a foreseeable disaster from crossing into another country 's airspace . Canadians , per capita , may be more guilty than most of Earth 's citizens , given the amount of fuel we burn -- a family member visiting from Australia this week was gob-smacked by the sheer number of gas-guzzling pickups in driveways across rural Ontario -- but then , we 're in good company with the Americans , who are equally complicit in warming the planet . In the meantime , we can do a better job with forest management , informed by Indigenous knowledge , to avert or mitigate wildfire disaster .

@@139180271 <p> Brain disorders are now the leading cause of illness and disability , affecting over one-third of the world 's population . As the population continues to grow and age , this burden is expected to further increase in the coming decades . Therefore , brain health has become a global priority . Healthy dietary change is now recognized as a key strategy to improve population health since poor diet is a major contributor to the global burden of disease . <p> Healthy dietary choices , especially eating much less animal products , would also contribute greatly to environmental sustainability and climate change mitigation . The world 's consumption of animal products significantly contributes to environmental pollution through methane emissions , water contamination , and land degradation , making cattle farming a major ecological concern . Cows are major producers of methane , a potent greenhouse gas approximately 23 to 28 times more effective than carbon dioxide at trapping heat over a century . Globally , given that there are over 1.5 billion cows , 1.3 billion sheep , 14 billion chickens , and 1 billion pigs worldwide , livestock @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with cattle contributing the majority . Their manure contaminates rivers and streams with pathogens and organic matter , leading to algal blooms , oxygen depletion , and the death of aquatic life . Cattle farming also drives deforestation , particularly in regions like the Amazon , to create pastureland or grow feed crops such as soybeans . <p> Therefore , one potential path to reduce the impact of global climate change involves a significant change in the human diet . In 2019 , the EAT -- Lancet Commission ( a collaboration between a science-based global platform for food system transformation and The Lancet , a leading medical journal ) proposed the Planetary Health Diet to promote both human and environmental health ( Willett and team , 2019 ) . This diet mainly consists of plant-rich foods , such as whole grains , fruits , and vegetables , and only small amounts of animal-based foods . <p> Previous studies have shown that adherence to the Planetary Health Diet resulted in a decreased risk of cardiovascular disease , hypertension , asthma , and mortality . A recent study investigated whether the Planetary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Li and team , 2026 ) examined a large dataset from the UK Biobank ( Sudlow and team , 2015 ) to determine the relationship between the Planetary Health Diet and brain disorder risk . <p> They reported that the highest adherence to the Planetary Health Diet was associated with a 12% , 13 % , 13 % , and 19 % lower risk of stroke , depression , anxiety , and multimorbidity , respectively , and had a significant role in decelerating biological aging . Their analyses discovered an inverse relationship between the Planetary Health Diet and these common brain disorders . The link between the Planetary Health Diet and brain disorder risk was more pronounced in adult males under 65 years of age . The mechanistic reasons why compliance with the Planetary Health Diet lowers brain disorder risk are not fully understood ; however , this diet shares many features of the Mediterranean diet that are also associated with prevention of cardiovascular disease and cognitive aging . The dietary components of both diets are rich in antioxidants and polyphenols that have the potential to inhibit neuroinflammation in relation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from the gut microbiome and systemic circulation to read more about this topic , see : Your Brain on Food . <p> There are , however , some important caveats that should be considered . The authors estimate that over one billion people worldwide may not be able to afford the EAT -- Lancet diet ( Springmann and team , 2021 ) , and iron and zinc inadequacies and deficiencies are common among individuals with high consumption of plant-rich foods ( Beal and team , 2023 ) . However , these findings provide convincing evidence that it is possible to reduce brain disorder risk , slow down age-related decline , and advance food system sustainability to reduce global climate change . 
@@139180291 <h> What Is the Post-Truth Era and Is There Any Truth to It ? <h> Critically thinking about how we engage informational sources . <p> The " post-truth era " refers to a current trend in the zeitgeist , particularly in the media and political landscapes , in which it has been speculated that emotional appeals and personal beliefs have become more influential on public opinion than facts . <p> I say zeitgeist here because I 'm not convinced that such speculation spreads across all of society in a manner that infiltrates " good-thinking " people . People with a basic understanding of epistemology are aware that facts should outweigh emotions and beliefs as sources of evidence , and , as good thinking still exists , I 'm confident that this refers to the many , if not most . <p> However , that does n't mean that post-truth has n't infiltrated a larger-than-it-should cohort or that we might see " good thinkers " fall prey to such post-truth approaches more often than they should . However , I do think the potential for this speculation to have weight is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ issue . So , I think ' zeitgeist ' is a good fit -- the spirit of this unfortunate possibility is certainly manifest in the background of things . <p> With that , we 've seen the use of emotional appeals and the exploitation of personal beliefs for decades , if not centuries , in political argumentation and media representation . Why ? It works . I still remember those starving children that Sally Struthers spoke about in the ' 80s and ' 90s . Even the smartest among us are susceptible to falling for such strategies when the conditions are right ( at least , in terms of implicit influence ) . Acknowledgment of such strategies ' power to shape opinion is not new and certainly pre-dates the suggested 2016 start date of the " post-truth era , " though I think 2016 is worth mentioning because it also corresponds with the first uses of the phrase fake news . <p> What does the post-truth era really mean ? Is it an explanation for all the poor thinking presented in ' social ' settings over the past while ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? Is it a condemnation of what thinking and sourcing evidence is becoming ? Or is it implying that this is just the nature of things now and that we 're as well just accept it ? I 'm hopeful that it 's a mix of the first two ... <p> And why the focus on media and politics ? Whatever you want to say about politics ( and regular readers of this blog will know I dislike politics ) , the focus on media is perhaps most interesting because the issue may be what 's amplifying the effects of other considerations . That is , over the past 10-20 years , we 've gradually seen the decline of traditional new media . While there are still ' real ' journalists out there , they represent the minority , given that anyone can be a journalist these days , just as long as they have access to the internet . Buy a website or find a similar platform , start a blog and spew whatever beliefs , opinions and attitudes you have , as if they were factual . Damn @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sources , there remained an element of journalistic integrity with reporting , even if there was a slant to the message that came across . But now , when anyone can post whatever they want and dress it up like a credible media source , there 's a lot more room for misinformation , disinformation , and generally creating partisanship in societal and political views . Such developments also occur at a time where the internet , particularly social media algorithms , curates personalised experiences for each of its users - echo chambers of perspectives that create collections of siloed information . You see what you like , which may conflate how ' shared ' such a perspective might be . Likewise , you see things that you hate ( i.e. rage bait ) , thus reinforcing your positive association with the things you do like - strengthening the belief in a bi-partisan reality . There does n't seem to be room anymore for centrist political views or reasonable discussion between groups on social media . <p> While I 'd argue that the scope of ' post-truth ' can apply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that most things can be politicised ; and media simply acts a vehicle for information-sharing regarding such topics . For example , if a new scientific finding is released , it may inspire , open up more questions and potential research ; or , it may get shot down because it ' seems ' counter to one 's beliefs that are often linked with a political ideology ( e.g. cosmological research , human biology and climate change research ) , despite affecting everyone regardless of belief or political ideology . Likewise , media can grossly bastardise what scientific findings imply and sensationalise it to sell copies/subscriptions . <p> The critical thinker would say , if you 're interested in learning about what the new research says , read the original article . But , as I discussed in a previous post on this blog , who actually does that ? We want our information fast , because that 's what the internet/social media has normalised for us -- now and quickly . So , we misinterpret the research . We buy into the sensationalisation , and we get the wrong @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ actual researchers and scientists communicate , they use cautious words like ' may ' , ' might ' , ' suggest ' , ' perhaps ' and ' potential ' because good science is rightfully cautious . That does n't sound confident . People like confident . They want assuredness . But that 's not what science is about . Science does n't prove anything ; rather , it suggests and indicates in light of findings . Be that as it may , further distrust in science and credible institutions grows . <p> Then we hear something that sounds right , something that we like , that is consistent with what we think already . It piques our confirmation bias . We accept it . We adopt a ' makes-sense ' epistemology . So , here we are . <p> So , what do we do ? As you 'd imagine from a blog about critical thinking , I 'm going to recommend that critical thinking is vital to overcoming the many negative implications associated with this ' post-truth era ' and that we need to make efforts to enhance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the ability to evaluate claims and the credibility of information sources go hand in hand . That 's what the public needs to do . But what can those who already think critically do ? What can experts , especially in science fields , do ? In addition to their research , they need to work to restore the trust of wider society . They need to work to communicate directly with them and work to improve the accessibility of the way they communicate . They need to work to make the ' post-truth era ' merely a blip in human existence .

@@139241861 <p> Glenn McGillivray is managing director of the Institute for Catastrophic Loss Reduction and adjunct professor of disaster and emergency management at York University . <p> When the wildfires get rolling , the armchair experts get trolling . <p> Every summer , as smoke from Canada 's boreal forest drifts across North American skies , a familiar chorus erupts online . Amateur fire commanders take to social media with seemingly obvious solutions : Why do n't we just send in more water bombers ? Why not just doze a perimeter around the fire ? Why is n't the government building access roads into the woods ? <p> When megafires rage across millions of hectares , it is tempting to view the problem as a failure of policy , preparation or resolve . But this perspective overlooks a fundamental reality : When high-intensity crown fires get going in Canada 's northern wilderness , the sheer physics of extreme fire behaviour renders standard human suppression tactics practically useless . <p> Understanding why these blazes are nearly impossible to extinguish is not a story of inadequate response . It is a sobering lesson @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of climate change and the physical limits of fire management . <p> To understand the wildfire challenge , one must first recognize that the boreal forest is not merely susceptible to fire . It is an ecosystem structurally designed to burn . Spanning over 550 million hectares across Canada -- about half of it tree-covered - the boreal landscape is overwhelmingly dominated by conifers , which are needled , andnot moist green leafy trees . Under hot , dry and windy conditions , these species essentially act as standing fuel . Ever throw an old Christmas tree into a bonfire ? <p> Far from being a tragedy for the landscape , fire is a vital evolutionary partner . Species like the lodgepole pine are explicitly adapted to fire . Their resin-sealed cones require intense heat to open , release seeds and regenerate the forest . The boreal forest does not just endure fire , it was created by it and relies on it . <p> Much of the public 's frustration stems from a misunderstanding of how wildland firefighting actually works . Hollywood has popularized the image of the super-scooper @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inferno , instantly saving the day . <p> In reality , air tankers do not extinguish massive wildfires . Water and red-dyed suppressant drops are used primarily to cool down the blaze , while chemical retardants are laid ahead of a fire 's path to slow its progression and buy time . The actual work of putting out a fire falls to ground crews digging lines and extinguishing hot spots . <p> In the vast Canadian north , however , ground crews face an insurmountable barrier : access . As a general rule remote wildfires are usually triggered by lightning strikes , while human activity drives many of the fires that are closer to where people live , work and play . Nationally , the breakdown is about an even 50/50 . <p> To construct a massive network of roads and bridges across thousands of miles of boggy wetlands and steep terrain to reach every remote lightning strike would be both financially and logistically astronomical , as well as ecologically absurd . <p> Even if every fire were accessible , the sheer volume of concurrent blazes creates a crisis of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , hundreds of active wildfires burn simultaneously across the country ( more than 900 are burning today ) . <p> Managing a challenge of this magnitude quickly exhausts a finite supply of specialized personnel , heavy equipment and aircraft . Transporting crews , gear and fuel into the roadless wilderness creates severe logistical bottlenecks . Furthermore , because climate change is lengthening fire seasons worldwide , neighbouring provinces and international partners are increasingly tied up with their own emergencies , limiting the availability of mutual aid . <p> The battle against massive boreal crown fires can not be won through brute force . <p> Recognizing the limits of human intervention is not an admission of defeat ; it is a prerequisite for sensible policy . Rather than demanding that crews conquer nature 's most violent blazes , we must focus our resources strategically where they matter most , safeguarding human lives and communities while allowing the boreal forest to carry out its ancient , necessary cycles .

@@139242889 <h> As loon chicks become less common , Birds Canada turns to Muskoka volunteers to help the iconic bird <p> Birds Canada photo by Missy Mandel . The Canadian Lake Loon Survey is one of Birds Canada 's longest-running citizen science programs , relying on volunteers to monitor common loon nesting success throughout the summer . <p> Muskoka 's lakes are some of the most important breeding habitats for common loons anywhere in the world , but Birds Canada says the iconic birds are raising fewer chicks than three decades ago , making the actions of local cottagers , anglers and boaters more important than ever . <p> The findings come from Birds Canada 's Canadian Lake Loon Survey , a volunteer monitoring program that has tracked loon nesting success on thousands of lakes for more than 40 years . While Ontario has not seen the steep declines recorded in Atlantic Canada , researchers say the long-term downward trend in chick production highlights the need to protect lake habitat and reduce human disturbance . <p> What is the Canadian Lake Loon Survey and how does it work ? <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ longest-running citizen science programs , relying on volunteers to monitor common loon nesting success throughout the summer . By tracking how many chicks loon pairs raise each year , researchers can measure the birds ' reproductive success and identify long-term trends in lake health and environmental change . <p> Since launching in Ontario in 1981 , more than 4,000 volunteers have monitored loon pairs on roughly 4,500 lakes , recording whether adults successfully hatch and raise chicks . <p> " We 're asking people to continue the survey so that we can keep track of what 's going on and doing our best to remind people that they have an impact , " said Kathy Jones , volunteer manager and biologist with Birds Canada . <p> Jones said the survey is designed for " enjoying your lake , " encouraging residents and cottagers who spend several days each summer at the same lake to take part . Volunteers only need to check on loon activity a few times each month to contribute valuable data . <p> As Muskoka has a number of lakes throughout the region , Jones explains loons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cottagers apt candidates for survey participation . <p> Registration for this year 's survey is open until Aug. 1 . Anyone who signs up after that date will participate beginning next summer . <p> To register for the Canadian Lakes Loon Survey , click here . To make a donation to Birds Canada , click here . <p> What is the state of common loons , and what is causing their decline ? <p> Birds Canada explains that loons are in trouble . Their productivity has declined from 0.7 young per loon pair per year to 0.55 in recent years . If productivity falls below 0.48 per pair yearly , Birds Canada warns that populations will likely begin to decline . <p> Within their findings , Birds Canada states decline in loon productivity over time has been steepest in the Atlantic Provinces , where numbers have dropped below 0.48 young per pair per year . <p> Ontario , B.C. , and Prairie provinces have had shallow declines in productivity , but still remain above worrisome numbers . <p> Although loons are not decreasing at the same rate as less common @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " adding they are just as important to our ecosystem . <p> Reduced water clarity , generally linked to climate change , is among the greater concerns for the productivity and livelihood of young loons , according to Jones . <p> Loons are visual hunters that rely on clear water to spot and catch fish . When lakes become cloudier -- because of algae growth , increased boating activity or changing rainfall patterns linked to climate change -- adult loons have a harder time finding food , leaving chicks undernourished and less likely to survive their first winter migration . <p> Human disturbances and how you can help protect common loons <p> Though many environmental factors impact loon productivity , human disturbances are just as damaging to these birds ' survival . <p> " We have a lot of responsibility for loons , " said Jones , adding that Ontario is the biggest producing loon location in the world . <p> " Cottagers , and boaters , and anglers all want the same thing ; they want that clear , pristine , Muskoka lake that they can go and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Jones . " To keep that we have to work for it . " <p> If you are unable to participate in the Canadian Lakes Loon Survey , there are various steps to take while visiting the lakes this summer that could help protect loons . <p> Jones suggests improving shorelines and uplands on your property . <p> Programs such as Love your Lake offer shoreline naturalizing services to offer a healthier and more environmentally productive shoreline . <p> Jones said healthy upland areas are just as important as healthy shorelines . Replacing grass with native plants or bird gardens creates habitat for insects that fish eat , helping support the entire lake ecosystem . <p> She added that lawns provide little value for pollinators and can increase runoff into lakes , contributing to poorer water quality . <p> For boaters , Jones also encouraged them to slow down when travelling parallel to shorelines and reserve wake sports for deeper areas away from shore . She said large wakes can erode shorelines , stir up sediment and reduce water clarity , ultimately affecting the habitat loons rely on . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and discarded fishing gear . Monofilament line , ropes , hooks and plastic left behind can entangle or injure loons and other wildlife . She also recommends reeling in a lure and moving to another location if a loon begins chasing it .

@@139295492 <h> On prediction markets , people are betting big money on climate disasters <p> When heavy smoke from Ontario 's wildfires drifted down south people on Polymarket placed their bets on when New York 's dangerous air quality would improve , wagering nearly US$54,000 in three days.Eduardo Munoz/Reuters <p> The heavy smoke from Ontario wildfires drifted down to New York City this month and turned the sky a hazy orange . Pickup soccer games were cancelled . Public libraries and local police stations handed out face masks . And over on Polymarket , people placed their bets on when New York 's dangerous air quality would improve , wagering nearly US$54,000 in three days . <p> Prediction markets make it exceptionally easy for users to gamble on the outcome of real-world events . These online platforms -- led by the two biggest , Polymarket and Kalshi -- have exploded in popularity over the past year . In mid-2025 , their combined monthly volume of global bets totalled US$2-billion , according to the Pew Research Center . By this April , it was closing in on US$24-billion . <p> The vast @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , such as the winner of the World Cup ( US$5.7-billion wagered ) or the next prime minister of Ethiopia ( US$229-million and change ) . But there are now options to put money on weather disasters , too . <p> Among them : Will a Category 5 hurricane hit the United States this year ? Will an 8.0-magnitude earthquake strike the world this month ? What about an earthquake in L.A. before 2027 ? Or in Japan before 2030 ? What about sea ice in the Arctic -- will it retreat by more than 5 million square kilometres before summer is up ? <p> Last year , people gambled almost US$240-million just on Kalshi 's climate-related markets . They 're on pace to pass US$1-billion by the end of 2026 . <p> And while prediction markets have been largely off-limits for Canadians , who can only access the U.S.-based platforms by disguising their location with a virtual private network , Kalshi has partnered with Wealthsimple on an app coming this year . Sports bets wo n't be allowed on Wealthsimple Predict . But climate-related trades will . <p> During @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ads of Croatian soccer star Luka Modric betting on high temperature records.KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI/AFP/Getty Images <p> " The number of extreme weather disasters are on the rise . The impacts on people are on the rise , " said climate researcher Katharine Hayhoe , chief scientist of the Nature Conservancy . " So if you 're looking for something getting worse and worse that gives you more and more chances to bet , I 'm very sorry to say climate change offers those opportunities . " <p> Kalshi has n't exactly been shy about drawing that connection . The Gulf of Maine is still warmer than it was historically , but compared to the most recent very warm years , now is " kind of a nice reprieve " for marine species that prefer cooler water , Bachman said . <p> Scientists attribute these temperature swings in large part to the competing influences of the warm Gulf Stream ocean current coming from the south and the Labrador Current coming from the north . Over the past two years , the Gulf Stream has had less of an influence on New England waters , but it appears to be coming back , according to the State of the Ecosystem report . <p> Temperature changes are scrambling where different species live . " <p> Scientists expect the lobster population even in Maine waters to decline from now on . " The bluff begins with prominent members of the state , media and industry making extravagant claims about the ability of an emerging technology to foster " progress . " Their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the technology creates more problems , requiring a new agenda to solve them and initiating another cycle of the technological bluff . " Lulled by the bluff of technological discourse , " warned Ellul , " we sleepily fail to perceive the perils that confront us . " <p> Now we 've been told by Carney and Smith that CCUS is key to ridding the world of carbon emissions by 2050 , building a new Canada and accelerating innovation . @@139339902 <h> To find the root of Canada 's wildfire emissions , look below the trees : study <p> Most of the carbon emitted by Canada 's record 2023 wildfires came not from burning trees , but from peat and soil , according to a new study that warns a warming climate is making the country 's vast underground carbon deposits increasingly vulnerable to fire . <p> The study says it estimates , for the first time , that about 76 per cent of those emissions came from burning peat and soil , while the rest was trees and other aboveground vegetation . <p> As wildfires become larger and more intense , long-term carbon stored in peatlands and soils could become a growing source of greenhouse-gas emissions , the study warns , contributing to a feedback loop in which global warming fuels fires and fires fuel further warming . <p> Those fires have prompted criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump , who blamed Canada 's forest management for cross-border smoke and used the issue to threaten new tariffs . But co-author Alemu Gonsamo , a McMaster University researcher , says the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ much of what 's burning lies underground , better managed forests wo n't necessarily solve the core problem : only steep cuts to global emissions can , he said . <p> " There is no alternative than reducing the greenhouse gas emissions , " said Gonsamo , an associate professor at McMaster who studies how forest ecosystems respond to climate change . <p> The study estimates the 2023 fires burned about 150,000 square kilometres and released roughly three times as much carbon dioxide as Canada 's total annual reported greenhouse-gas emissions . <p> To figure out how much of that came from soil and peat , the researchers trained a machine-learning model on 20 years of data from a NASA field project in Alaska and Western Canada measuring actual wildfire conditions . The team then applied that model to data from across Canada . <p> This ground-up approach produced similar findings as other researchers who estimated total emissions by instead working backwards from what showed up in the atmosphere . <p> Monday 's study found peatlands were responsible for about 33 per cent of those emissions . Peatlands store large @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ decomposition and allow for the buildup of organic matter over thousands of years . <p> But hotter and drier conditions fuelled by climate change can dry out peatlands , making it more vulnerable to burning <p> " Now , some of this carbon is released in just one week in a large fire , the carbon that took millennia to accumulate in the ecosystem , " he said . <p> The study also has its limitations , Gonsamo said . Most of the field data used to train the model came from Western Canada and Alaska , with fewer observations from Central and Eastern Canada . He also noted that estimating soil combustion is challenging because researchers rely on indirect indicators , such as moisture conditions , rather than direct observations of what 's burning underground . <p> " We need more data , more ground measurements in Eastern Canada and generally in many parts of Canada to represent all the ecosystems in Canada that potentially can burn , " he said .
