@@139377933 <p> When 's the last time you really looked at a pigeon or locked eyes with a squirrel ? <p> You 'll be forgiven if you ca n't remember ; after all , synanthropy -- the phenomenon of wild animals and other organisms living in human environments -- has been a part of our species ' story since well before recorded history . There 's evidence dating back 30,000 years , to the Pavlovian cave culture of northeastern Europe , of ravens and foxes living as companions to humans at a time when the world was mired in a prolonged ice age and our main prey was the woolly mammoth . <p> Times have changed . Humans now cluster in the millions in cities instead of in the hundreds in caves , and we 're facing the daunting prospect of a heating planet rather than one covered in glaciers . But one thing has n't changed : Our homes are still overrun by animals . <p> This is n't just a turn of phrase . Long derided as " biological deserts , " urban ecologists have discovered over the past @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the areas that surround them . That makes cities not just places where animals and plants end up living , but legitimate ecosystems in their own right , as important as any other across this vast planet . And they 're getting more important by the day . <p> As extreme weather events intensify around the world , animal species across North America are facing compounding threats to their survival . The amplification of wildfires , floods and droughts may be terrifying for human communities , but they can be apocalyptic for animal ones . When they strike , animals must often flee to safer spaces , which are often cities or towns . <p> Meanwhile , the abundance of food waste , small prey , and regulated temperatures that animals encounter when they arrive in these urban spaces can also end up keeping them there , creating new synanthropes -- wild urban creatures -- in the process . Along with continued urban sprawl , which traps formerly free-roaming animals in fragmented human-centred habitats , this churn is making cities wilder every single day . <p> According to a team @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Marc T.J. Johnson , thousands of species are predicted to move into cities over the coming decades , adding immense complexity to urban ecosystems that are already brimming with life . What 's more , across the 60 most populous cities across the continent , nine of the top 10 into which animals are most likely to be moving are in Canada , including Quebec City , Ottawa , Halifax , Laval , Edmonton , Montreal , Winnipeg , Brampton , and Calgary ( number 11 on the list is Toronto ) . That 's set to turn Canada into a veritable synanthrope hotspot . In the most extreme ( and hopeful ) scenario , the team predicts that Quebec City alone will become home to 500 more species , while Calgary will see over 250 more resident animals . <p> A modern paradox is that living in an urban space is a key cause of biophobia , despite the fact that cities and towns are among the most biodiverse places in the world.Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press <p> The emerging ecological recognition of cities as ecosystems is further proof of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and towns means interacting daily with animals . In Toronto , estimates place the number of raccoons at anywhere between 100,000 and 640,000 , meaning that a veritable raccoon city exists within its human one . That ubiquity has transformed Toronto into a place defined by its legions of bandit-masked scavengers . In Vancouver , evening is punctuated not just by the setting sun over the Pacific Ocean but by the " evening murder " : the daily migration of the city 's 10,000 crows back to their nesting grounds in Still Creek , Burnaby . In Halifax , like so many places , coyotes are a common fixture in the forests and urban spaces across the peninsula , surprising families and joggers in Clayton Park , Spryfield and Point Pleasant Park . <p> Finding yourself face to face with an animal means feeling scared , or joyful , or surprised , or meditative , or suddenly very much aware of the vulnerability of your soft flesh . It also means feeling momentarily elevated out of your daily rhythm and the imposing constraints of your quotidian life . Animals can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . What 's more , neither scientists nor spiritualists can quite explain why . So while studies have demonstrated that hearing birdsong relieves anxiety and paranoia in humans when they hear it , the reasons that it does so is beyond our understanding . <p> This has all led to a curious situation : we both fear animals while yearning to be around them . It 's a reflection of our broader feeling of social isolation along with a rising " biophobia " -- a fear of nature itself -- resulting from our increasing sense of disconnection from the natural world . Ecologists have also found that biophobia can reduce a person 's support for pro-biodiversity initiatives while increasing their antagonism to nature , which ultimately acts as a drag on efforts to reduce global warming and climate-related catastrophes . The paradox here is that living in an urban space is a key cause of biophobia , despite the fact that cities and towns are among the most biodiverse places in the world . <p> The startling emergence of a new class of urban animals during the Great Urban Shift @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ natural world . If so , that would surely push back against the rising tide of biophobia -- and that could n't come at a more critical moment . <p> While the Great Urban Shift is causing thousands of new species to gain footholds in our neighbourhoods , their survival is no guarantee . Faced with hostile urban environments , and cut off from others of their kind , many species are too vulnerable to existing predators or too slow to adapt to the unique puzzles of urban spaces . That 's borne out in the most dire models predicted by biologists who study the Great Urban Shift . In the worst-case scenarios , where global warming , habitat destruction , and fossil fuel extraction accelerate , cities could see a net reduction of species instead of a gain . And because many of the species predicted to move into cities are rare or threatened ones , cities may be becoming extinction graveyards : places where an endling -- the last remaining member of a threatened species -- is most likely to succumb to the void forever . <p> As @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into urban spaces is finally illuminating one of the most obscure features of the climate crisis : the dynamics of mass extinction . The International Union for the Conservation of Nature , which tracks the vulnerability of the world 's flora and fauna , has identified 49,500 species currently at risk of extinction . While that might sound large , it only includes organisms that biologists have actually identified . The true count , it turns out , is likely more than one million , meaning that humanity is only aware of a paltry five per cent of all of the species that might be lost forever . Scientists have been hard-pressed to record these human-driven extinctions because most happen far from our prying eyes . <p> But the rise in synanthropy is changing that calculus . Biologists are now studying animals as they make their way toward extinction ( a process called " extinction debt " ) right in the heart of some of the world 's largest cities , rather than in remote rainforests and jungles . In Canada , that includes the Little Brown Myotis , an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other cities , and which has been decimated by white nose fungus . Or Blanding 's Turtle , a long-necked reptile found across towns from Ontario to Nova Scotia that is a frequent victim of vehicle collisions . Meanwhile , all across Canada , monarch butterflies -- brilliant migratory insects -- are declining as the amount of urban green space dwindles . <p> None of these extinctions are inevitable . What 's more , unlike trying to contend with the massive global forces of climate change , transforming cities from future sites of mass extinction into sustainable and healthy ecosystems is n't an abstract fight . All it takes is opening our eyes to the fact that our cities are teeming with life , and then acting on the many pragmatic strategies we have to sustain the species that surround us . <p> These include low-cost approaches like planting pollinator-friendly native plants wherever possible , or ensuring that there are enough " stepping stones " ( green spaces as large as parks or as diminutive as plant-covered traffic medians ) across cities to give animals multiple paths to rest and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ networked green roofs -- essentially , rooftop gardens -- across downtown cores , which have the dual benefit of serving as habitats for bird and bat species while also reducing the high temperature of urban spaces . Wildlife corridors , protecting wetlands and forests , and the creation of wildlife crossings all take energy , advocacy and funding , but they too are achievable goals for cities and towns committed to sustaining biodiversity . <p> All of these solutions , though , necessarily begin with a recognition that our urban spaces are worthy sites of conservation . So next time you hear scratching in your walls or birdsong on your block , take a moment to recognize that nature is no distant entity . Wherever you live -- and especially if it 's in an urban centre -- you are , every day , a participant in a grand and complex ecosystem . That recognition is a fine place to start the next phase in our collective efforts to stave off mass extinction .

To avoid preventable fires , officials ban campfires , restrict the use of heavy machinery and sometimes prohibit the use of off-road vehicles . But before making those decisions , they need to determine just how bad the fire danger is in the first place . <p> Many people may be familiar with fire danger ratings from online maps or signs stationed at provincial parks , outside local fire halls and on highways leading into small towns . <p> The billboards , with their green , yellow , orange and red markers that denote different fire danger levels , are simple signs , but there 's a century 's worth of science behind them . And the fire risk they communicate affects how people live and work in B.C. <p> Industrial activities in dry forests and grasslands are responsible for a chunk of B.C. 's human-caused fires , and as the fire danger climbs , workers face increasing restrictions . <p> When fire danger is high , the B.C. government @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hours after using grinders , chainsaws or other cutting tools that might produce a spark . The same rules apply to mowing the grass along a right-of-way , felling trees with a machine or a number of other risky activities within 300 metres of forest or grasslands . <p> Fire danger maps , like these from July 17 and 27 , respectively , show where the fire risk is highest . Higher fire risk brings restrictions on industry . Images via BC government . <p> Once the fire danger hits " extreme , " high-risk activities are restricted to morning hours . If the fire danger remains extreme for more than three days , those activities are banned all day long . <p> Higher fire danger often means restrictions for the general public as well . Lists of these restrictions can be found online and typically involve things like campfire bans and sometimes even limits on backcountry recreation . <p> Just how flammable is this forest ? <p> Forest fire danger rating research began in Canada in the 1920s with studies in experimental plots to investigate the moisture content and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and twigs that litter the forest floor to the deeper organic layers below . Over time , researchers incorporated that work into a series of scientific models now used across Canada and around the world to estimate wildfire danger and fire behaviour . <p> Fire agencies across the country rely on the national Fire Weather Index System to help determine the fire danger ratings communicated to the public through the familiar roadside signs and online maps . <p> The system pulls temperature , relative humidity , wind speed , wind direction and rainfall data from automatic weather stations dotted across the country . That data is then fed into models that estimate the dampness of the forest floor at different depths . <p> Think about the forest after it rains . <p> " You walk around , it 's squishy and wet -- you 're not going to be able to start any fires , whether you want to or not , " Daniel Perrakis , a fire research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service , explained . But the material beneath one 's feet can quickly dry out in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ system shines , " Perrakis said . It essentially allows fire managers to track the wetting and drying of the forest floor through three different measures : the fine fuel moisture code , the duff moisture code and the drought code . <p> Daniel Perrakis and other scientists use a range of measures to predict fire behaviour after a spark hits the forest floor . Photo supplied . <p> The fine fuel moisture code reflects the estimated moisture content of the top layer of needles , grasses and twigs . That topmost layer , Perrakis told The Tyee , is the " most volatile . " It dries out or moistens the fastest as the weather changes , and the code is a key metric for understanding the flammability of fine fuels . <p> On July 21 , for instance , as a new fire grew from a spark to more than 4,000 hectares outside the B.C. community of Boston Bar , the fine fuel moisture code in the area hit the top of the scale , reflecting the extreme volatility of the local forests . <h> RELATED STORIES <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the decayed leaves , needles and twigs just below the surface layer and is particularly useful to determine the flammability of medium-sized branches or other woody debris and the decayed matter a few inches below the surface . <p> The third measure , the drought code , reflects the moisture content in the deep organic layers and is used to assess the potential for a fire to burn large logs and to smoulder deep into the ground . <p> The three fuel moisture codes help determine two other key ratings -- the Initial Spread Index and the Buildup Index -- that help experts estimate how fast a fire could spread if ignited and how much fuel would be available to burn . <p> In turn , those two ratings determine the Fire Weather Index , a single number meant to reflect the intensity of a fire spreading through a pine forest . As that number increases , fire danger ratings shift from low to extreme , green to red , with slight variations across the country . <p> For decades , the Fire Weather Index was typically updated once @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ released a new hourly version that Perrakis says does a better job tracking the moisture of the forest floor and changes in wind over the course of a day . <p> The new version also allows managers to model fire weather in grasslands , as well as the standard pine forest . <p> " In a grassland , if it rained two days ago but it 's hot and dry today , basically all the effects of that rain are gone , " Perrakis explained . The grassland model is more reactive to changes in the weather . <p> The BC Wildfire Service , like other fire agencies across the country , uses the Fire Weather Index System to inform wildfire management decisions . <p> But it will be a few years before the service adopts the new hourly system , Rick van Kesteren , a fire information officer with the BC Wildfire Service , said in a statement to The Tyee . <p> " We are collecting data on the Fire Weather Index system and analyzing its performance through the fire season , but a lot of work is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ said . <p> For now , the service still relies on the codes and indexes in the old model to forecast potential fire starts each day . <p> When it comes to deciding when to ban campfires , the service relies on the Buildup Index , the measure of fire-ready fuel in each area . Thresholds vary across B.C. regions , depending on the kinds of forests or grasslands found in the area . <p> The fire service issues a campfire ban when half the weather stations in the area exceed that threshold . <p> Municipalities , meanwhile , typically issue their own fire restrictions , which apply within their boundaries . They may align with the BC Wildfire Service orders for the broader region , but they can also be different , accounting for a community 's unique risks . <p> In the district of North Vancouver , where hillside communities are nestled right up against dense coastal forests , the changing fire danger ratings used to come with " an enormous amount of work , " fire chief Mike Danks told The Tyee . <p> Different fire danger @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ public signage to be deployed across the community . <p> " We were just chasing our tail with this , constantly trying to keep up with it , " he said . <h> BC Needs to Be More Proactive About Highway Closure Warnings <p> In response , West Vancouver , the city and district of North Vancouver , and Metro Vancouver made the decision to ban open burning and campfires across the North Shore . <p> " When you look at the trend with climate change , the risk of wildfire , people are hypersensitive about it here on the North Shore -- and charcoal is a risk , " Danks said . <p> " We have been super proactive within the fire service to ensure that all of our staff are trained in wildfire response , " he said , noting they recently sent crews to support the BC Wildfire Service in Boston Bar . @@139378409 <p> At this hospital though , it 's not your vitals that will be examined , but your feelings . <p> The " Hospital of Emotions " is an immersive art experience that explores different facets of being human inside the long-shuttered St. Vincent Medical Center near downtown Los Angeles . <p> The former hospital was founded in 1856 by the Daughters of Charity religious order to treat poor people before it went bankrupt in 2020 and was bought by private investors . The site will be redeveloped into a homeless shelter and mental health and drug treatment facility , with the first phase opening later this year . <p> But until the end of September , the hospital rooms are filled with 80 installations by 70 artists . Each artist received around $14,000 to transform four floors of clinical space into explorations of feelings around everything from medical and family trauma to grief over climate change and immigration detention centers . <p> As in Pixar 's " Inside Out , " color-coded creatures sprinkled throughout the show personify a range of emotions from joy and hope to anger and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nurse 's station , while dueling green giants symbolizing jealousy face off in an otherwise normal exam room , their faces decorated with absurd , clownlike expressions . <p> IV bags are full of rainbow-colored liquids , overhead exam lights are festooned with a canopy of artificial flowers , and crutches are draped with campy , cartoonish wigs . <p> Enter the " Resilience Department " and you 'll find a prismatic , glass butterfly that refracts light , accompanied by an unsettling interactive audio piece about an artist 's experience having an epileptic seizure . The sound of grunts and labored breathing in headphones contrasts with screams , recorded and replayed in the room to create a surreal , out-of-body effect . <p> In the neighboring room , a thousand sunny-side up eggs are splayed all over the bed , walls and floor , which the artist , Melan Allen , said represent the eggs she was forced to eat during her childhood despite hating them . The room especially resonated with Sharon Maxwell , who drove from San Diego to see the show . <p> " I have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I 'm in recovery from an eating disorder , so I 've been in treatment , I 've been in hospitals . It 's all very sterile . " <p> While going to the hospital can be an isolating experience , Maxwell said visiting an art show in one made her feel a renewed sense of connection . There are n't nurses , surgeons or patients here , and everyone is on equal footing as viewers . <p> " Being the person in the bed , being treated for mental health stuff , you 're kind of like a spectacle , " she said . <p> A sensitive look at anxiety , fear and trauma <p> In the " Fear Department , " a virtual character based off a real person gives a vulnerable speech about post-traumatic stress from serving in a combat zone and then reads a suicide note that combines multiple veterans ' experiences using AI . The installation is titled " The Ward That Never Closed . " <p> <p> EDITOR 'S NOTE -- This story includes discussion of suicide . If you or someone you know @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988 . There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org <p> <p> Down the hall , another room is covered floor to ceiling in black-and-white portraits drawn with frenetic lines by an artist who spent 15 months at a U.S. immigration detention center . <p> " I left Russia in 2022 because of my political views and because I am gay . What I thought would be a search for safety became a prolonged encounter with fear , " Grisha Stepanian said . <p> His installation examines " how fear settles into the body , how it stays , even when there is no immediate danger . How safety , when it appears , feels temporary , almost unreal . " <p> The most successful rooms play with the visual language of a medical space without prescribing what to feel . <p> In another room in the " Fear Department , " artist Dongpu Ling created an eerie installation of transparent figurines -- molded from packing tape -- to bring a vision of her grandfather 's to life . He died years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ his hospital bed just before dying . <p> Torqued into myriad positions , the blank-faced figures occupy gurneys and disappear into institutional-gray ceiling vents . The work was also informed by Ling 's experience as a child spending 10 days in the hospital with a fever . <p> " I almost died . I could n't eat , " she said . " I threw up blood three times a night . " <p> The process of creating the installation was intense , Ling said . When she tried to go to her studio room and accidentally went to the basement , where bodies are typically stored before going to funeral homes , she said she found something chilling : " It was freezing cold and dead silent . " <p> Recognizing a paradox of emotions <p> Ondrea Boggs , an ultrasound tech , said the installations reminded her of people 's tenacity and resilience even in the face of death -- something she witnessed working in an intensive care unit and emergency room . <p> " I 'm confronted with people struggling every day and getting through and being @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when she sees a patient or their family able to stay hopeful during a difficult time . <p> " It 's encouraging for me to remember that that 's possible , " she said . " Even amongst moments of sadness you can still experience joy , it 's not like an isolated experience where you have to get through the sadness to experience joy , right ? Both can be shared at the same time and both can be honored . " <p> For other visitors , the installations also reflected that paradox of emotions . <p> " There 's solace in someone else seeing our emotion -- whether it 's joy and celebration or sorrow and pain . There 's something about the human experience where we need to be seen , " Maxwell said . " This art exhibit really shows that in a profound way . I think it put humanity on display in a really powerful way . "
